Crivella, an IURD bishop and Macedo's nephew, was a senator (2003–2016), Minister of Fishing and Aquaculture under Dilma Rousseff (2012–2014) and mayor of Rio (2017–2020). Police arrested him at home on 22 December 2020, nine days before his term ended, in an investigation into a kickback scheme in his administration, and he was suspended from office. He has sat in the federal Chamber of Deputies since February 2023.
cite: Rio de Janeiro state prosecutors and courts, arrest of 22 December 2020; Wikipedia 'Marcelo Crivella'

n: Marcos Pereira — Universal Church bishop as minister and party chief
rank: Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services; president of the Republicanos party; vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Republicanos was founded in 2005 by pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, and commentators describe it as a base from which the church's bishops run for office. Marcos Pereira, an IURD bishop, was Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services under Michel Temer (2016–2018), has led the party since 2018 and has been a federal deputy and vice-president of the Chamber since 2019. The party holds about 40 of 513 Chamber seats and 4 of 81 Senate seats, and São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas is a member.
cite: Wikipedia 'Republicanos' (party history and officeholders)

n: Frente Parlamentar Evangélica — 132 deputies and 14 senators sign on
d: The Frente Parlamentar Evangélica is a registered cross-party caucus in Brazil's Congress that votes as a bloc on issues its churches care about. Agência Pública counted 93 federal deputies tied to evangelical churches in the 2023–2027 Chamber, led by the Assemblies of God (25) and Baptists (15), with the Universal Church among the three largest groups. The front's vice-president, Cezinha de Madureira, said in February 2023 that it brought together 132 deputies and 14 senators; signatories need not be evangelical themselves.
cite: Agência Pública, 'As igrejas que dominam a nova ala evangélica na Câmara', February 2023

n: Kim Kataguiri — MBL leader linked to Atlas partner, now federal deputy
d: The Atlas Network is a US-based network that funds and trains free-market think tanks worldwide. In April 2015 Atlas described Kim Kataguiri, head of the Movimento Brasil Livre (MBL) that led street protests against President Dilma Rousseff, as working with its Brazilian partner Estudantes Pela Liberdade, and said 'many members' of the MBL had passed through its training programme. Kataguiri was elected to the federal Chamber of Deputies in 2018 and re-elected in 2022.
cite: Atlas Network, 'Students For Liberty Plays Strong Role in Free Brazil Movement', 1 April 2015

n: MIRA — Colombian party of the Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ
d: The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International is a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia with branches in many countries. The MIRA party (Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation), founded in 2000 by Carlos Alberto Baena and Alexandra Moreno Piraquive, lists the church as its religion. The party currently holds 3 Senate seats, 1 seat in the House and 47 local council seats.
cite: Wikipedia 'Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation'

n: Javier Milei — Atlas Network prize-winner as President of Argentina
d: Before entering politics Milei won the Liberty Prize of Fundación Atlas in 2018, sat on the advisory board of Fundación Libre and spoke at events of Atlas Network partners Fundación Libertad y Progreso and Federalismo y Libertad; his adviser Alberto Benegas Lynch is a Mont Pelerin Society director active in several Atlas groups (DeSmog, August 2023). Milei took office in December 2023. In August 2025 the Atlas Network credited its Argentine partners Libertad y Progreso, Fundación Libertad and the Asociación Argentina de Contribuyentes with helping push his deregulation, tax and labour reforms; these are the network's own claims.
cite: DeSmog, 22 August 2023; Atlas Network, 'Sharpening Milei's Chainsaw', 29 August 2025

n: Horacio Cartes — US cites ties to Hizballah, sanctions later lifted
rank: former President of Paraguay; serving Vice-President Hugo Velázquez
d: Hizballah is a Lebanese armed movement and party that the US designates as a terrorist organisation; it has long-standing finance networks in South America's Tri-Border Area. On 26 January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and sitting vice-president Hugo Velázquez for corruption, stating that both 'have ties to members of Hizballah', that Hizballah 'regularly held private events in Paraguay', and that representatives of both men collected bribes at those meetings. The US removed the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025.
cite: US Treasury, press release JY1221, 26 January 2023 (E.O. 13818); OFAC delisting reported by WorldECR, October 2025

n: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — ordered to trial over Iran pact
d: In 1994 the AMIA Jewish centre in Buenos Aires was bombed, killing 85 people; Argentine courts charged Iranian officials. In 2013 President Fernández de Kirchner's government signed a memorandum with Iran on questioning the suspects, which prosecutor Alberto Nisman denounced as a cover-up before his death in 2015. A trial court dismissed the case, saying the pact was not a crime, but the Federal Court of Cassation ordered a trial, and on 5 December 2024 the Supreme Court upheld that order, so she must stand trial for aggravated cover-up.
cite: Supreme Court of Argentina, ruling of 5 December 2024 (El Cronista)
org_note: Government of Iran (AMIA bombing suspects)

n: Rafael López Aliaga — Opus Dei member as mayor of Lima
d: Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation whose lay members seek holiness in ordinary work; it has long had members in Latin American governments. Rafael López Aliaga, leader of the Renovación Popular party, describes himself as an Opus Dei member who keeps celibacy. He was mayor of Lima from 1 January 2023 until he resigned on 13 October 2025 to run for president; he came third in the April 2026 first round with 11.91% and was elected to the national Senate, taking office in July 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rafael López Aliaga' (Opus Dei membership and offices)

n: Eduardo Arana — Peru's prime minister and a Masonic lodge hire
rank: President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister); earlier Minister of Justice
d: In July 2025 the TV programme Cuarto Poder reported that Prime Minister Eduardo Arana reportedly holds the 33rd degree of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, and that while he was Justice Minister a lodge member, Elías Falla Villegas, was hired as a consultant in November 2023 at S/15,600 a month, while another reputed lodge member's foundation received an official certification at a July 2024 ceremony Arana attended. Arana said membership of a private association was no grounds to assume favours and that the hire met the job's requirements. No lodge was named.
cite: Canal N, 7 July 2025, citing Cuarto Poder (América TV)

n: José Antonio Kast — Schoenstatt-raised President of Chile
d: Schoenstatt is a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914 by priest Josef Kentenich and active in more than 100 countries, with nearly 80 of its shrines in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. BBC Mundo reported that Kast and several siblings were raised under Schoenstatt's guidelines; his brother Miguel Kast, Pinochet's planning minister and Central Bank president, was the only other member to hold high office in Chile. Kast won the 14 December 2025 runoff and took office on 11 March 2026.
cite: BBC Mundo, 18 December 2025 (republished by Acento)

n: Russian Interior Ministry training centre in Managua — US sanctions
d: Russia's Interior Ministry opened a police training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua in October 2017, attended by Russia's ambassador and Laureano Ortega Murillo, the president's son; it was set up as an affiliate of the Russian ministry, with courses for Nicaraguan police and later for Central American and Caribbean officers. On 15 May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned the centre, saying it trains Ortega-Murillo government officials under the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society.
cite: US Treasury sanctions, 15 May 2024 (La Prensa, Nicaragua); Confidencial, 25 October 2017
org_note: Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs

n: Chinese police 'service stations' listed in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador
rank: overseas outposts attributed to Chinese county and city police bureaus
d: Safeguard Defenders' 2022 reports listed Chinese police outposts in Rio de Janeiro (Qingtian County police) and São Paulo (Fuzhou city police), and also in Buenos Aires, Viña del Mar in Chile, and Guayaquil and Quito in Ecuador. The group said Chinese police recorded 230,000 fraud suspects 'persuaded to return' between April 2021 and July 2022. A Yale legal scholar found factual errors in the first report, which the group then revised. No Latin American government has announced findings on these sites.
cite: Safeguard Defenders, '110 Overseas' (September 2022) and 'Patrol and Persuade' (December 2022); Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

n: Sanae Takaichi — Nippon Kaigi Diet league member becomes PM
d: Nippon Kaigi (Japan Conference) is Japan's largest nationalist lobby group, founded in 1997, with about 38,000–40,000 members; it works on politicians through a cross-party league of Diet members. Sanae Takaichi has served in that league, as The Japan Times reported in 2021. She won the Liberal Democratic Party leadership in October 2025 and was elected prime minister by the Diet on 21 October 2025, at the head of an LDP–Japan Innovation Party coalition. She still holds the office.
cite: The Japan Times, 5 September 2021; Wikipedia summary of Nippon Kaigi and of Takaichi's election

n: Takaichi cabinet — 10 of 19 ministers in Nippon Kaigi's Diet league
d: On 23 October 2025 Japan Press Weekly, the English service of the Communist Party paper Akahata, listed the affiliations of the new Takaichi cabinet appointed on 21 October. It named 10 ministers as members of the Nippon Kaigi lawmakers' league: Hiraguchi Hiroshi, Motegi Toshimitsu, Katayama Satsuki, Matsumoto Yohei, Ueno Kenichiro, Kaneko Yasushi, Ishihara Hirotaka, Kihara Minoru, Akama Jiro and Kiuchi Minoru. In Abe's 2014 cabinet the count reported was 15 of 19. Takaichi reshuffled the cabinet in September 2026; the count for the reshuffled cabinet was not checked.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — 12 ministers in the Shinto Political League
d: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Political League) is the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines and runs a league of Diet members who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported on 23 October 2025 that 12 ministers of the new Takaichi cabinet belonged to its Diet league, among them Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki and Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru. Seven of them were also listed as Nippon Kaigi league members.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — five ministers with Unification Church ties
d: The Unification Church (Family Federation for World Peace and Unification) is a Korean-founded church whose ties to LDP lawmakers came to light after Shinzo Abe's killing in 2022; Tokyo courts ordered its Japanese branch dissolved in 2025. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported on 23 October 2025 that five ministers of the new Takaichi cabinet had ties to it. It listed Matsumoto Yohei (a party branch he headed paid dues to the church-linked Women's Federation for World Peace, revealed in 2019), Ueno Kenichiro (paid fees to affiliated bodies in 2018–19 and attended an affiliated lawmakers' meeting in 2021), Akazawa Ryosei and Ishihara Hirotaka (spoke at affiliated meetings) and Kiuchi Minoru (sent a congratulatory telegram to an affiliated company's event in 2018).
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Komeito quits LDP coalition after 26 years
d: Komeito is the party founded in 1964 by the leader of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, whose members supply its votes. It governed with the LDP from 1999 to 2009 and from 2012 to 2025. On 10 October 2025 Komeito leader Tetsuo Saito announced the party was leaving the coalition, citing disagreements with Sanae Takaichi's leadership and the LDP's handling of its slush-fund scandal. Takaichi then formed a coalition with the Japan Innovation Party, and Komeito is now in opposition.
cite: Komeito announcement, 10 October 2025 (NHK, CNBC); Wikipedia: Komeito

n: TM report — church backed 290 LDP lawmakers in 2021 election
d: In January 2026 South Korean media, citing Unification Church documents seized in Korean investigations, reported that Eiji Tokuno, then head of the church's Japan branch, told leader Han Hak-ja that the church backed 290 LDP members in the October 2021 lower-house election. The LDP's own 2022 survey had found 179–180 of its lawmakers with ties to the church. The same documents are reported to describe Abe as pleased with church support at a meeting before the 2019 upper-house election. Akahata separately reported that an August 2021 'TM Special Report' to Han said Takaichi becoming LDP president would be 'Heaven's greatest wish fulfilled'.
cite: Jiji Press, 2 January 2026, citing South Korean media; Akahata/Japan Press Weekly, January 2026

n: Chun Jae-soo — oceans minister quits over Unification Church money
d: Chun Jae-soo, a Democratic Party lawmaker serving as President Lee Jae-myung's oceans minister, resigned on 11 December 2025. Yun Young-ho, former head of the Unification Church's world headquarters, told the special counsel investigating ex-first lady Kim Keon-hee that the church gave Chun 30 million won in cash and two luxury watches in 2018–2020 to seek his help with a Korea–Japan undersea tunnel project. The special counsel passed the matter to police, who booked Chun as a bribery suspect and barred him from travel. Chun denies the allegations.
cite: Reuters/The Star, 11 December 2025; Korea JoongAng Daily, 15 December 2025

n: Hu Peng-nien — retired Executive Yuan official jailed for united front
d: China's united front system works to win over or recruit people abroad, including in Taiwan, for the Communist Party. In September 2026 Taiwan's High Court sentenced businessman Cheng Ming-chia to 10 years and six months for building a network for Communist Party united front officials, arranging meetings in China from 2021 to 2025. It sentenced Hu Peng-nien, a retired official of the Executive Yuan (Taiwan's cabinet), to five years. Prosecutors said Hu tried to recruit military personnel and others for information on the military and on government and legislative work, and carried a Chinese-supplied communications device into Taiwan. Both rulings can be appealed.
cite: Taiwan High Court ruling (Taipei Times, 11 September 2026)

n: Solomon Islands — MPs say both Beijing and Taipei offered money, 2019
d: In September 2019 Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of diplomatic ties with Taiwan and recognised the People's Republic of China. The Guardian and the Solomon Star reported that MPs said both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars to sway the vote. Riots over the switch followed, and anger over it was a factor in the violent unrest in Honiara in November 2021.
cite: The Guardian and Solomon Star reporting, 2019; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations

n: Solomon Islands — China-funded PM's fund paid 39 of 50 MPs
d: China agreed in 2019 to fund a discretionary fund run by the Solomon Islands prime minister's office, as Taiwan had done before. At a livestreamed parliamentary budget committee hearing in August 2022, the prime minister's secretary Jimmy Rodgers said China had provided SBD20.9 million (about US$2.49 million) spent in 2021, and that 39 of the 50 MPs received payments in two tranches, on 22 November and 13 December 2021. Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote in December 2021; opposition leader Matthew Wale accused him of using the money to stay in power, which Sogavare's office denied.
cite: Parliamentary budget committee hearing, August 2022 (Reuters via VOA, 25 August 2022)

n: Chinese police inside Solomon Islands policing
d: China sent its first police advisory team to the Solomon Islands in February 2022, after the November 2021 riots, and signed a security agreement in 2022 that lets Honiara ask for Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese Ministry of Public Security police in the country began a local pilot of the 'Fengqiao' model of community surveillance policing; it was suspended after local objections. In May 2026 Matthew Wale, a critic of the China relationship, became prime minister and promised to review the security agreement.
cite: East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations

n: Kiribati — Chinese uniformed police working with local force
d: Kiribati switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked China for policing help in 2022. Kiribati's acting police commissioner Eeri Aritiera confirmed to Reuters in 2024 that up to a dozen uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside local police on six-month rotations, doing community policing, martial-arts training and IT support for a crime database.
cite: Kiribati Police Service statement to Reuters (NBC News, 2024)

n: Vanuatu — China's public security minister offers policing pact
d: China has sent police advisers to Vanuatu since 2023. On 19 September 2025 Vanuatu's internal affairs minister Andrew Solomon Napuat met China's Minister of Public Security Wang Xiaohong in Beijing; China donated police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones, and the two sides said they were discussing a wider policing partnership.
cite: Pacific Media Network, 23 September 2025; East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024

n: Fiji — Chinese officers removed from police, 2011 pact kept
d: Under a 2011 police cooperation agreement signed during military rule, China's Ministry of Public Security attached two officers at a time to the Fiji Police Force from 2013 and posted a police liaison officer to its embassy in 2021. In 2017 Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw its embedded officers but would keep the agreement, reviewing it every six months, and Fijian officers continue to train in China.
cite: Fiji Home Affairs Minister, ABC interview (BenarNews/RFA, 20 March 2024); East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024

n: Jian Yang and Raymond Huo — two MPs leave over China concerns
d: Jian Yang, a National Party MP from 2011 to 2020, had been a Communist Party member and taught at People's Liberation Army institutions that trained intelligence linguists before moving to New Zealand. Several outlets reported in 2021 that his retirement at the 2020 election came after intelligence agencies raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government. The same reports said Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and opposition leader Todd Muller agreed that Labour MP Raymond Huo would also leave Parliament for the same reason.
cite: New Zealand media reports, 2017 and 2021; Wikipedia: Jian Yang

n: Huang Jing — Singapore expels LKY School professor as foreign agent
rank: foreign-policy academic (target: Singapore foreign policy and opinion)
d: On 4 August 2017 Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs cancelled the permanent residence of Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the National University of Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, and of his wife, and banned both from re-entering. The ministry called him 'an agent of influence of a foreign country' who worked with that country's intelligence agents to influence Singapore's foreign policy and public opinion. It did not name the country. Huang denied the charge.
cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs statement, 4 August 2017
org_note: prc_state is used because the case is widely read as China, but Singapore's ministry did not name the country

n: Philip Chan — Singapore's first 'politically significant person'
d: Singapore's Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate people at risk of being used by foreign actors, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. On 26 February 2024 the ministry designated Hong Kong-born businessman Philip Chan Man Ping, the first person listed. He was president of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and the Kowloon Club, a patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies, and had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a united front body, as an overseas delegate. The ministry said he had shown he was susceptible to being cultivated by foreign actors.
cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs designation, 26 February 2024

n: Alice Guo — Bamban mayor jailed for life over POGO trafficking
d: POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed in the Philippines from 2016 that served players in China; Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban, Tarlac in 2022, was linked by senators to the Zun Yuan Technology POGO hub raided in her town; the Ombudsman removed her from office on 13 August 2024 and barred her from public office. In June 2025 a Manila court voided her election, ruling she is a Chinese citizen, Guo Hua Ping, born in Fujian. On 20 November 2025 she was convicted of qualified human trafficking and sentenced to life in prison. A self-confessed Chinese spy, She Zhijiang, told Al Jazeera she was also a Chinese intelligence asset; she denies it and that claim is untested in court.
cite: Ombudsman decision, 13 August 2024; Manila RTC Branch 34, June 2025; trafficking verdict, 20 November 2025

n: Harry Roque — ex-presidential spokesman charged over POGO hub
d: Harry Roque was spokesman for President Rodrigo Duterte, under whom POGOs were legalised and expanded. In May 2025 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court, Branch 118, issued arrest warrants for Roque, businesswoman Cassandra Ong and 48 others on 11 counts of qualified human trafficking over Lucky South 99, a POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, raided in June 2024. Prosecutors say Roque helped it seek a licence and was named as head of its legal department in a reapplication that the gaming regulator PAGCOR denied. Roque denies being its lawyer and has sought asylum in the Netherlands.
cite: Angeles City RTC Branch 118 arrest warrants (GMA News, 15 May 2025)

n: Philippines bans POGOs after Senate inquiry
d: The state gaming regulator PAGCOR licensed offshore gaming operators from 2016, and President Duterte declined China's 2019 request to shut them. After 2024 Senate hearings led by Risa Hontiveros and Sherwin Gatchalian, President Marcos announced a total ban in July 2024 and signed Executive Order 74 in November 2024 requiring all operations to stop by 31 December 2024. Congress made the ban law in the Anti-POGO Act, signed in October 2025.
cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order No. 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025)

n: Chen Zhi — Prince Group head, adviser to Hun Sen, indicted in US
rank: adviser to Hun Sen and other leaders
d: Chen Zhi, born in Fujian, took Cambodian citizenship in 2014 and built the Prince Group, one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates. He held the honorary title Neak Oknha and served as an adviser to Hun Sen, interior minister Sar Kheng and National Assembly president Heng Samrin. On 14 October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him for fraud and money laundering, calling him the head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds, seizing about 127,271 bitcoin (about US$14 billion), while the US and UK sanctioned 146 people and firms linked to the group. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China to face charges.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment and OFAC/UK sanctions, 14 October 2025; Cambodian government statement, January 2026

n: Huione — firm co-run by PM Hun Manet's cousin named a laundering hub
rank: prime minister's cousin, director of Huione Pay
d: Huione Group is a Phnom Penh financial conglomerate whose payment arm Huione Pay has Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director. In March 2025 the National Bank of Cambodia revoked Huione Pay's banking licence. In May 2025 the US Treasury's FinCEN found Huione Group to be a financial institution of primary money laundering concern, saying it laundered over US$4 billion in illicit funds between August 2021 and January 2025, including money from North Korean hackers and scam operations.
cite: FinCEN finding, 1 May 2025; National Bank of Cambodia, March 2025

n: RSS roots — 38 of 53 BJP ministers in Modi's second government
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925; the governing Bharatiya Janata Party grew out of its political wing. ThePrint counted in January 2020 that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Narendra Modi's second government (71%) had RSS roots, up from 41 of 66 (62%) in 2014. All eight members it listed on the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, including Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah and Nitin Gadkari, had RSS links; Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar did not. It also counted 146 of 303 BJP Lok Sabha members with RSS links.
cite: ThePrint, 27 January 2020

n: C. P. Radhakrishnan — RSS member since 16, now Vice President
d: C. P. Radhakrishnan has been associated with the RSS and its earlier political wing, the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, since the age of 16, and later served as a BJP MP for Coimbatore and as governor of several states. He was elected the 15th Vice President of India and took office on 12 September 2025. The vice president also chairs the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.
cite: Wikipedia: C. P. Radhakrishnan (citing Indian press)

n: Canada expels six Indian diplomats over use of Bishnoi gang
d: Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in Surrey, British Columbia on 18 June 2023. In October 2024 the RCMP said 'agents of the Government of India' had used criminal groups, including the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, who is held in an Indian prison, to target pro-Khalistan Sikhs in Canada, and Canada expelled six Indian diplomats including High Commissioner Sanjay Kumar Verma. India denies involvement and expelled Canadian diplomats in return. Canada listed the Bishnoi gang as a terrorist entity in September 2025, and in July 2026 US prosecutors charged Bishnoi with directing Nijjar's killing; that indictment does not allege an Indian government role.
cite: RCMP statement and Global Affairs Canada expulsions, October 2024; Canada terrorist-entity listing, September 2025

n: Pannun plot — Nikhil Gupta pleads guilty; RAW officer charged
d: US prosecutors charged that Vikash Yadav, an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the foreign intelligence agency RAW, directed a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen and lawyer for the pro-Khalistan group Sikhs for Justice, in New York in 2023. His go-between, Nikhil Gupta, agreed to pay $100,000 to a hitman who was really an undercover officer, with a $15,000 cash advance on 9 June 2023. Gupta was extradited from the Czech Republic in June 2024 and on 13 February 2026 pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to murder-for-hire, conspiracy and money-laundering conspiracy. Yadav was charged in a superseding indictment unsealed in 2024 and has not been brought to the US.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of New York: Gupta guilty plea, 13 February 2026
org_note: The Indian state's intelligence service is the actor; the brief allows state cases where named in the task

n: Gnanasara — BBS leader named to head 'One Country, One Law' task force
d: Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012, accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence. On 26 October 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed its general secretary, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a presidential task force on 'One Country, One Law' to draft proposals on a single legal code. Justice Minister Ali Sabry said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said the task force would take over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.
cite: Presidential gazette, 26 October 2021 (Daily FT)

n: Gnanasara — presidential pardon voided, BBS leader back in prison
d: In 2018 the Court of Appeal jailed BBS leader Gnanasara for six years for contempt of court during the case over the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda; President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. He was jailed again for four years in March 2024 over statements about Islam, and for nine months in January 2025 for inciting religious hatred. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court declared the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid, and on 5 October 2026 the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of the contempt sentence.
cite: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026; Court of Appeal order, 5 October 2026

n: Gotabaya Rajapaksa — defence secretary opens BBS training centre
d: On 9 March 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, brother of President Mahinda Rajapaksa, opened Meth Sevana, the Bodu Bala Sena's cultural and training centre in Galle District, as chief guest. In January 2013 President Rajapaksa and ministers met BBS leaders at the official residence, Temple Trees. Gotabaya Rajapaksa later served as president from 2019 to 2022.
cite: Colombo Telegraph, 14 March 2013; Wikipedia: Bodu Bala Sena

n: Ma Ba Tha drafts become Myanmar's race and religion laws
d: Ma Ba Tha (Association for the Protection of Race and Religion) is a Buddhist nationalist monks' group formed in 2014. In 2013–14 Myanmar's Ministry of Religious Affairs drafted four Race and Religion Protection Laws, covering religious conversion, marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men, monogamy and birth spacing, based on texts proposed by its members. Parliament passed them in 2015, the first being signed in May 2015.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 29 May 2014; Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha

n: Myanmar army spokesman donates to banned Ma Ba Tha successor
d: Myanmar's state Buddhist clergy council ordered Ma Ba Tha disbanded in May 2017, and officials said its renamed successor was also outlawed. In June 2019, after members protested the civilian government's sedition case against the monk Wirathu, army spokesman Brigadier General Zaw Min Tun donated 30 million kyats to the successor group, the Buddha Dhamma Parahita Foundation. Zaw Min Tun is now the spokesman of the military government that took power in 2021.
cite: Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha (citing Myanmar press)

n: Wirathu — junta drops sedition case and gives him top honour
d: Wirathu is a monk of the 969 movement and a leading figure of Ma Ba Tha, known for anti-Muslim sermons. In September 2021, seven months after the coup, the military government dropped the sedition charges against him and released him. In November 2022 he was awarded the title Thiri Pyanchi, one of the country's highest honours.
cite: Military government announcements, 2021–22; Wikipedia: Wirathu

n: Vietnam designates exile party Viet Tan a terrorist group
d: Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. On 4 October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute the designation; the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership.
cite: Vietnam Ministry of Public Security, 4 October 2016

n: Eva Kaili — EP vice-president charged in Qatargate
d: Qatargate is a Belgian criminal case into cash paid to people in the European Parliament to favour Qatar and Morocco. On 9 December 2022 Belgian police arrested Greek MEP Eva Kaili, then one of the Parliament's 14 vice-presidents; bags of cash were found at her home and a suitcase of cash with her father. Parliament removed her as vice-president on 13 December 2022 by 625 votes to 1. She is charged with corruption, money laundering and membership of a criminal organisation and denies the charges; in February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the investigation had been lawful, so the case continues.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office (investigating judge Michel Claise); European Parliament vote of 13 December 2022; Brussels Court of Appeal ruling, February 2026

n: Fight Impunity — NGO used as channel for Qatar and Morocco cash
rank: former MEP and chair of the EP human rights subcommittee
d: Fight Impunity was a Brussels human-rights NGO founded by former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, who had chaired the Parliament's human rights subcommittee. Police found about €600,000 in cash at his home in December 2022. Panzeri's former assistant Francesco Giorgi told investigators that payments from Qatar and Mauritania were routed through the NGO; Panzeri signed a plea deal with Belgian prosecutors in January 2023 to tell what he knew. Prosecutors say Morocco's foreign intelligence agency (DGED) agreed in 2019 to pay Panzeri and Giorgi €50,000 a year each to lobby for Morocco.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; Panzeri plea agreement, January 2023; Financial Times and Der Spiegel reporting on the case file

n: Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino — immunity lifted in Qatargate
d: In February 2023 the European Parliament lifted the immunity of Belgian MEP Marc Tarabella and Italian MEP Andrea Cozzolino at Belgium's request. Tarabella, vice-chair of the delegation for relations with the Arabian Peninsula, was arrested and charged with corruption and money laundering; he denies wrongdoing. Cozzolino, long-time chair of the delegation to the Maghreb countries, was arrested in Naples on a Belgian warrant on 10 February 2023. Neither stood again in 2024; Tarabella was re-elected mayor of Anthisnes in October 2024.
cite: European Parliament immunity votes, February 2023; Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office

n: Huawei bribery probe — European Parliament offices searched
d: Huawei is a Chinese telecoms company with a large lobbying office in Brussels. In March 2025 Belgian prosecutors arrested several people and searched offices inside the European Parliament on suspicion that, since 2021, gifts, travel and football tickets were given in exchange for political positions favouring Huawei. On 18 March 2025 four people were charged with active corruption and membership of a criminal organisation and a fifth with money laundering; the number charged later rose to eight. Parliament banned Huawei lobbyists from its buildings and the European Commission stopped meeting groups that speak for Huawei.
cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office statements, 13 and 18 March 2025; European Parliament and European Commission decisions, 2025

n: Huawei probe — immunity waiver sought for three sitting MEPs
d: In May 2025 European Parliament President Roberta Metsola passed on Belgian requests to lift the immunity of MEPs Fulvio Martusciello (Italy, Forza Italia), Nikola Minchev (Bulgaria) and Daniel Attard (Malta) in the Huawei bribery case. One of Martusciello's staff had been arrested in Naples in March 2025 on a European arrest warrant. Belgian prosecutors later said the Daniel Attard who received gifts was a namesake, the mayor of Għasri, and in June 2026 Parliament voted not to lift the MEP's immunity.
cite: European Parliament plenary announcements, May 2025; Parliament vote on Attard immunity, June 2026

n: Bystroň follow-up — European Parliament lifts his immunity (2025)
rank: AfD member of the Bundestag, then MEP
d: Voice of Europe was a Prague-based news site that Czech intelligence exposed in March 2024 as a Russian-funded influence network run for Viktor Medvedchuk, paying European politicians. German prosecutors in Munich suspect AfD politician Petr Bystroň of taking cash or crypto from it in return for speaking and voting in Russia's interest. The Bundestag lifted his immunity in 2024 and police searched his offices; after he became an MEP, the European Parliament lifted his immunity again on 6 May 2025 by a large show of hands. Bystroň denies the allegations.
cite: Munich Public Prosecutor's Office; Bundestag immunity decision 2024; European Parliament plenary vote, 6 May 2025

n: Nathan Gill — ex-MEP jailed for Medvedchuk-network bribes
rank: Member of the European Parliament (UKIP/Brexit Party), later Reform UK leader in Wales
d: Nathan Gill sat in the European Parliament for Wales from 2014 to 2020. In September 2025 he pleaded guilty to eight counts of bribery between December 2018 and July 2019: Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn paid him to make pro-Russian statements in the Parliament and on Ukrainian TV channels, passing on requests from 'V', said in court to be Viktor Medvedchuk. On 21 November 2025 the Old Bailey sentenced him to 10 years and 6 months in prison.
cite: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey), sentence of 21 November 2025; Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command investigation

n: Tatjana Ždanoka — MEP investigated as Russian FSB contact
d: Tatjana Ždanoka, co-chair of the Latvian Russian Union, sat in the European Parliament from 2004 to 2024. In January 2024 leaked emails published by The Insider and partners showed her reporting to officers of Russia's FSB from at least 2004. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case on 22 February 2024 for possible cooperation with Russian intelligence and searched her property in July 2024; the European Parliament imposed a penalty on her in April 2024 for breaking its code of conduct.
cite: Latvian State Security Service (VDD) criminal case, opened 22 February 2024; European Parliament President's penalty decision, April 2024
org_note: Russian intelligence acting directly; org kept generic

n: Béla Kovács — Jobbik MEP convicted of spying for Russia
d: Béla Kovács sat in the European Parliament for the Hungarian nationalist party Jobbik. Hungarian prosecutors accused him of spying on EU institutions for Russia, and the European Parliament lifted his immunity on 14 October 2015. In September 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison for espionage; he lives in Russia.
cite: Curia of Hungary, judgment of September 2022; European Parliament immunity vote, 14 October 2015
org_note: Russian intelligence acting directly

n: Front National — €9m loan from First Czech Russian Bank
rank: national party leadership (Front National, now Rassemblement National)
d: In November 2014 Marine Le Pen confirmed that her party had taken a €9 million loan from the First Czech Russian Bank in Moscow. Party officials told Mediapart it was the first part of a €40 million package, which Le Pen disputed. She said French banks had refused to lend and that the money came from a private bank, not the Russian state; the party is now the largest group in France's National Assembly.
cite: Statement by Marine Le Pen, November 2014; Mediapart investigation

n: Lega — Metropol hotel talks on Russian oil money
rank: party (Lega) – aide to deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini
d: In 2019 a recording was published of an October 2018 meeting at Moscow's Metropol hotel where Gianluca Savoini, a Salvini associate and president of the Lombardy–Russia cultural association, discussed an oil deal meant to channel money to the Lega. Milan prosecutors investigated Savoini and others for international corruption. In April 2023 a Milan judge closed the case: the judge found the actions were 'unequivocally aimed' at illegally financing the party but the deal never reached the point where it could achieve that.
cite: Milan Public Prosecutor's Office investigation; dismissal order of the Milan preliminary-investigations judge, April 2023

n: Lega signs cooperation pact with Putin's United Russia
rank: party leader Matteo Salvini (later deputy prime minister)
d: United Russia is Vladimir Putin's ruling party. On 6 March 2017 Lega leader Matteo Salvini signed a ten-point cooperation agreement with it in Moscow, covering party delegations, links between Duma deputies and Italian legislators, and trade and investment. The pact runs for five years and renews unless one side gives notice; the Lega gave none, so Il Foglio reported it was tacitly renewed in March 2022 to run until 2027. Salvini is deputy prime minister in the current Italian government.
cite: Text of the Lega–United Russia agreement, published by Il Foglio, 30 July 2022

n: FPÖ's five-year pact with United Russia (2016–2021)
d: On 19 December 2016 the leadership of Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed an 'Agreement on Collaboration and Cooperation' with United Russia, covering delegation exchanges, legislative experience and economic ties. FPÖ ministers then sat in government from 2017 to 2019. The agreement expired at the end of 2021 when leader Herbert Kickl chose not to renew it, which United Russia's Andrey Klimov confirmed.
cite: FPÖ and United Russia statements; Vindobona report on the expiry

n: Nikolay Malinov — Russophile leader cleared of spying for RISS
rank: former member of parliament; leader of the Russophiles movement
d: The Russian Institute for Strategic Studies (RISS) is a Russian state think tank. Bulgarian prosecutors charged Nikolay Malinov, a former MP and head of Bulgaria's largest pro-Russia NGO, in 2019 with collecting state secrets for RISS between 2013 and 2019. While on bail in 2019 he travelled to Moscow, where Vladimir Putin gave him the Order of Friendship. A Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026.
cite: Bulgarian Specialised Prosecution Office indictment, 2019; Sofia court acquittal, May 2026

n: Gagauzia governor Evghenia Guțul jailed over Russian party funds
rank: Governor (başkan) of the autonomous region of Gagauzia
d: The Șor Party, led by businessman Ilan Shor, was declared unconstitutional by Moldova's Constitutional Court on 19 June 2023 for serving a foreign state's interests. Evghenia Guțul won the governorship of Gagauzia as its candidate in 2023 and met Vladimir Putin in March 2024. In August 2025 a Moldovan court sentenced her to seven years in prison for using undeclared Russian money to finance the party; the party's former secretary was sentenced at the same hearing for handing out 9.8 million lei to pay protesters.
cite: Constitutional Court of Moldova, decision of 19 June 2023; Chișinău court sentences, 5 August 2025

n: Jian Guo — Krah's EP aide jailed for spying for China
d: Jian Guo, a German citizen of Chinese origin, worked as an assistant to AfD MEP Maximilian Krah. He was arrested in April 2024 and on 30 September 2025 the Dresden Higher Regional Court sentenced him to 4 years and 9 months for working for China's Ministry of State Security, including passing on information about European Parliament business. The Bundestag lifted Krah's own immunity on 11 September 2025 and police searched his homes and offices in Berlin, Dresden and Brussels.
cite: Dresden Higher Regional Court judgment, 30 September 2025; Bundestag immunity vote, 11 September 2025

n: Frank Creyelman — Flemish ex-senator paid by China's MSS
rank: former Belgian senator and Flemish MP (Vlaams Belang)
d: Frank Creyelman sat in the Belgian Senate (1999–2007) and the Flemish Parliament (2007–2014) for Vlaams Belang. On 15 December 2023 a joint investigation by the Financial Times, Der Spiegel and Le Monde reported that for three years he took money from an officer of China's Ministry of State Security to influence debate in Europe. Vlaams Belang expelled him; Belgian police investigated but reported that a gap in Belgian criminal law prevented prosecution.
cite: Financial Times / Der Spiegel / Le Monde joint investigation, 15 December 2023; Vlaams Belang expulsion

n: Christopher Cash — parliamentary researcher's China spy case dropped
rank: parliamentary researcher; director of the MPs' China Research Group
d: Christopher Cash worked as a researcher for Conservative MP Alicia Kearns and directed the China Research Group of Conservative MPs. He and Christopher Berry were charged under the Official Secrets Act 1911 with passing information about Westminster that investigators suspected reached senior Communist Party official Cai Qi. In October 2025 the Director of Public Prosecutions dropped the charges, a decision that became a political row in Westminster.
cite: Crown Prosecution Service charges, 2024, and decision to discontinue, 2025

n: Ye Jianming — CAIFC veteran as Czech president's adviser
rank: economic adviser to President Miloš Zeman
d: The China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC) is a Beijing 'friendship' body. Ye Jianming, chairman of the oil conglomerate CEFC China Energy, was its deputy secretary-general from 2003 to 2005. Czech President Miloš Zeman made him an economic adviser (from 2015 per some sources, January 2017 per others) while CEFC bought Czech assets. Ye was detained in China in March 2018 and Shanghai state investors took over CEFC.
cite: Czech Presidential Office statements; Reuters and Fortune reporting on CEFC

n: Ireland orders China's Dublin 'police station' to close
d: In September 2022 the human-rights group Safeguard Defenders reported that police bureaus in Chinese cities ran unofficial 'overseas service stations' abroad, used to pressure people wanted by China to return. One was listed on Capel Street, Dublin, run for the Fuzhou city police. In late October 2022 Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs ordered it to close.
cite: Irish Department of Foreign Affairs order, October 2022; Safeguard Defenders report 'Patrol and Persuade', September 2022

n: Netherlands orders two Chinese 'police stations' shut
d: After the Safeguard Defenders report, the Dutch foreign ministry said two Chinese 'overseas service stations' in the Netherlands had been operating illegally because China never notified the Dutch government of them. Foreign minister Wopke Hoekstra ordered both closed and said the matter would be investigated further.
cite: Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, November 2022

n: Italy ends joint street patrols with Chinese police
d: Under an agreement with China, Chinese police officers had joined Italian police on patrols in Italian cities with large Chinese communities. Safeguard Defenders listed four Chinese 'police stations' in Italy (Rome, Milan, Florence, Prato). In December 2022 Italy said the joint patrols would end; interior minister Matteo Piantedosi said they were unrelated to the stations. A 2023 ProPublica investigation found the leaders of the Fuzhou police station in Prato had ties to organised crime.
cite: Italian Interior Ministry statement, December 2022; ProPublica investigation, 2023

n: Hungary agrees joint patrols with Chinese police (2024)
d: In mid-February 2024 Hungarian Interior Minister Sándor Pintér and China's Minister of Public Security reached a policing cooperation agreement that lets Chinese officers patrol alongside Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denied that Chinese police stations exist in Hungary; Safeguard Defenders had listed two in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts.
cite: Hungarian Interior Ministry statement, February–March 2024; Safeguard Defenders report, 2022

n: PACE corruption inquiry names members working for Azerbaijan
rank: members and a former president of the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly
d: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) brings together MPs from 46 national parliaments and monitors elections and human rights. An Independent Investigation Body chaired by a former president of the European Court of Human Rights reported in April 2018 that there were 'strong suspicions' of corruptive activity involving former PACE president Pedro Agramunt and that Luca Volontè and Azerbaijani member Elkhan Suleymanov had seriously breached the code of conduct. It found former German MP Eduard Lintner received €799,500 into personal accounts from Azerbaijan-linked companies and named breaches by members from Belgium, Germany, Poland, Romania, the UK and others. PACE then stripped several current and former members of rights and access.
cite: Report of the Independent Investigation Body on the allegations of corruption within the Parliamentary Assembly, 15 April 2018

n: Luca Volontè — ex-PACE group leader jailed for Azerbaijani bribes
rank: former Italian MP and leader of the EPP group in PACE
d: Luca Volontè led the centre-right EPP group in PACE. Milan prosecutors charged him in 2016 with taking €2.39 million from Azerbaijani officials, routed through companies, in return for support in the Assembly, The 2018 PACE investigation body found he played 'an important role in undermining' the Strässer report on political prisoners in Azerbaijan. In January 2021 the Court of Milan sentenced him to four years in prison for corruption.
cite: Court of Milan, judgment of January 2021

n: Bundestag lifts immunity of two CDU MPs over Azerbaijan money
rank: members of the Bundestag (CDU) sitting in PACE
d: In January 2021 the Bundestag lifted the immunity of CDU MP Karin Strenz, accused of taking at least €22,000 to lobby for Azerbaijan in PACE; she had already been fined in 2019 for not declaring Azerbaijani income. On 4 March 2021 it lifted the immunity of CDU MP Axel Fischer, under federal police (BKA) investigation for taking money from Azerbaijan. Former CSU MP and junior interior minister Eduard Lintner was investigated in the same case.
cite: German Bundestag immunity decisions, January and 4 March 2021; Munich prosecutors and BKA investigation

n: Azerbaijani Laundromat — $2.9bn via Danske Bank Estonia
rank: bank supervision; payments reaching sitting European politicians
d: In September 2017 the OCCRP and partner newspapers published 16,000 leaked bank transactions showing about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through four UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch. Almost half came from an Aliyev-linked account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan. Recipients included Bundestag member Karin Strenz and Slovenian MP Zmago Jelinčič, and payments reached people who defended Azerbaijan in PACE.
cite: OCCRP 'The Azerbaijani Laundromat' investigation, September 2017

n: Kosovo hands six Gülen-linked Turks to Turkey; spy chief jailed
rank: director of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency; interior minister
d: Turkey's government calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group and has sought its members abroad since the 2016 coup attempt. On 29 March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence seized five teachers and a doctor accused by Ankara of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, who said he had not been told, sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief. In 2023 the Basic Court in Pristina sentenced former intelligence chief Driton Gashi to four years and eight months for abuse of office over the deportations.
cite: Basic Court of Pristina judgment, 2023; Kosovo government dismissals, 30 March 2018
c_note: Kosovo is not in the canonical country list

n: Moldova's intelligence service hands seven Turkish teachers to Ankara
d: On 6 September 2018 Moldova's Security and Intelligence Service (SIS) detained seven Turkish teachers and managers of the Gülen-linked 'Orizont' school network and sent them to Turkey, saying they were suspected of ties to an Islamist group. In June 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Ozdil and Others v. Moldova that the arrests were neither lawful nor necessary and amounted to an illegal transfer to Turkey, and ordered Moldova to pay €25,000 to each applicant.
cite: European Court of Human Rights, Ozdil and Others v. Republic of Moldova, judgment of 11 June 2019

n: DITIB imams investigated for spying on Gülen followers
rank: imams paid as Turkish civil servants; imams working in German prisons and schools
d: DITIB runs about 900 mosques in Germany; its imams are trained in Ankara and paid as civil servants of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet. In 2017 German federal prosecutors investigated DITIB imams suspected of passing information on Gülen supporters in Germany to Turkish authorities, and police searched imams' homes. Several imams left Germany, and in December 2017 prosecutors dropped the case for lack of evidence and because some suspects were out of reach. North Rhine-Westphalia introduced security checks for imams working in state prisons.
cite: German Federal Prosecutor's Office investigation, 2017, closed December 2017

n: France dissolves the Grey Wolves by cabinet decree
d: The Grey Wolves (Ülkü Ocakları) are the youth movement of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), which governs Turkey in alliance with President Erdoğan. On 4 November 2020 the French Council of Ministers dissolved the movement in France, after an Armenian genocide memorial was defaced; Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin said it incited discrimination and hatred and took part in violent acts. The ban remains in force.
cite: French Council of Ministers dissolution decree, 4 November 2020

n: Austria bans the Grey Wolves salute and symbols
d: From 1 March 2019 Austrian law banned the Grey Wolves hand salute and symbols, with fines of up to €4,000. Turkey's foreign ministry condemned the ban because the symbol belongs to the MHP, a legal party in Turkey's governing alliance. In January 2020 four Vienna bus drivers were dismissed for making the sign.
cite: Austrian Symbols Act amendment in force 1 March 2019

n: French state report on Muslim Brotherhood 'entryism' in local politics
d: In May 2025 a report by two senior civil servants, commissioned by the government, was examined by President Macron's Defence Council. It called the Muslim Brotherhood a 'threat to national cohesion', said 'political Islamism' was spreading 'from the bottom up' at municipal level, and named the federation Musulmans de France (formerly UOIF) as the Brotherhood's national branch. The authors also wrote that no recent document showed a wish by Muslims in France to set up an Islamic state; Musulmans de France rejected the findings.
cite: French government report on the Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism, Defence and National Security Council, 21 May 2025

n: Austria's Operation Luxor raids later ruled unlawful
d: On 9 November 2020 Austrian authorities searched about 60 addresses and questioned 70 people suspected of belonging to Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas networks, terrorist financing and money laundering. In August 2021 the Graz Higher Regional Court ruled that the house searches were unlawful.
cite: Graz Higher Regional Court decisions, August 2021

n: UK proscribes Hizb ut-Tahrir (2024)
d: Hizb ut-Tahrir is an international party founded in 1953 that calls for a single caliphate; it is banned in Germany, Turkey, Russia, Pakistan, Indonesia and most Arab states. After years of debate, the UK government announced in January 2024 that it would proscribe the group as a terrorist organisation, and the ban took effect on 19 January 2024 after Parliament approved it. Membership or support is now a criminal offence in the UK.
cite: Terrorism Act 2000 (Proscribed Organisations) (Amendment) Order 2024, approved by Parliament January 2024

n: Germany bans the Islamic Centre Hamburg as Tehran's outpost
d: The Islamic Centre Hamburg, founded by Iranians in the 1950s, ran a large Shia mosque and was seen as aligned with Iran's government. In June 2022 Germany expelled its deputy director over ties to Hezbollah. In July 2024 the Federal Interior Ministry banned the centre as unconstitutional, closed the mosque and took the building under state administration; the centre's challenge was still pending at the Federal Administrative Court in 2025.
cite: German Federal Ministry of the Interior ban order, July 2024

n: Belgium refuses recognition to Brussels Great Mosque over Moroccan spies
d: The Great Mosque in Brussels' Cinquantenaire park was run under a Saudi lease until 2018. In December 2020 Justice Minister Vincent Van Quickenborne refused it state recognition unless its management changed, after Belgian intelligence reported that Morocco had placed its own people in charge and that three staff, including a director, were members of Moroccan intelligence. The Muslim Executive, Belgium's official Muslim body, was ordered to remove representatives of the Moroccan government.
cite: Belgian Federal Justice Ministry decision, December 2020
org_note: Moroccan state intelligence (DGED) using a religious institution

n: Pope forces out Order of Malta's Grand Master
rank: Prince and Grand Master of a sovereign order with UN observer status
d: The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that is recognised as a sovereign subject of international law and keeps its own diplomatic service. In December 2016 Grand Master Matthew Festing dismissed Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager over condom distribution in a charity project; Pope Francis set up an inquiry, Festing refused to cooperate, and in January 2017 the Pope asked him to resign. The Order reinstated Boeselager and the Pope named Archbishop Becciu as his special delegate. On 3 September 2022 Pope Francis promulgated a new constitution for the Order and made provisional appointments to its Sovereign Council; the Order's chapter confirmed most of them in January 2023.
cite: Holy See and Order of Malta statements, January 2017; papal decree promulgating the Order's constitution, 3 September 2022

n: Scientology under German domestic-intelligence watch
rank: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV)
d: Germany's government does not treat Scientology as a religion and says its aims run against the democratic order. The federal domestic intelligence service (BfV) and several state services have monitored it since 1997; in May 2008 Scientology dropped its legal fight against the surveillance after the Münster Higher Administrative Court refused to hear its appeal. A 2007–2008 attempt by interior ministers to ban it outright was abandoned for lack of legal grounds.
cite: North Rhine-Westphalia Higher Administrative Court (Münster), 2008; BfV annual reports

n: 'Loggia Ungheria' — secret-lodge claims against judges dismissed
rank: judges, CSM members and senior officials named by a witness
d: Lawyer Piero Amara told Milan prosecutors that a secret association, 'Loggia Ungheria', linked magistrates, officials and business people; he named more than 60 people. A Perugia judge closed the inquiry into the alleged lodge, and Milan prosecutors sent Amara to trial for slandering 65 people. The leak of his statements also led to the conviction of Piercamillo Davigo, a former member of the judges' governing council (CSM), for revealing official secrets; in December 2024 the Court of Cassation ordered a new appeal.
cite: Perugia preliminary-investigations judge (archiving order); Brescia court and Court of Appeal judgments 2023–2024; Court of Cassation, 4 December 2024
org_note: alleged lodge; investigators did not establish that it existed

n: Castelvetrano secret association — ex-Sicilian MP and speaker arrested
rank: former Sicilian regional MP; former president of the Sicilian Regional Assembly
d: On 21 March 2019 Trapani prosecutors and Carabinieri had 27 people arrested in a case that included the crime of forming a secret association, banned in Italy since the P2 scandal. Former regional MP Giovanni Lo Sciuto was alleged to have exchanged favours with an official of the INPS pensions office for disability pensions that delivered votes; former Sicilian Assembly president Francesco Cascio was placed under house arrest. Prosecutors said the group steered the Castelvetrano town council through its mayor and deputy mayor in 2012–2017.
cite: Trapani Public Prosecutor's Office; arrest order of the Trapani preliminary-investigations judge, March 2019

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: Macron makes first presidential visit to the Grande Loge de France
d: The Grande Loge de France is one of France's main Masonic bodies. On 5 May 2025 Emmanuel Macron visited it, the first visit by a French president, and asked Freemasons to act as 'ambassadors of fraternity' for the 120th anniversary of the 1905 law separating church and state; he also welcomed their role in the end-of-life bill debate. The Élysée published the visit; Macron is not documented as a member.
cite: Élysée Palace, official record of the visit, 5 May 2025

n: Jorge Fernández Díaz — Opus Dei member as interior minister
d: Opus Dei is a Catholic institution whose lay 'supernumerary' members follow its spiritual programme while working in ordinary jobs. Jorge Fernández Díaz, a Partido Popular politician, was Spain's interior minister in Mariano Rajoy's government from 2011 to 2016, in charge of the police and Guardia Civil. He is reported to be a supernumerary member of Opus Dei.
cite: Spanish press reporting compiled in Wikipedia biography

n: Paola Binetti — Opus Dei numerary in Italy's parliament
rank: Senator and member of the Chamber of Deputies (from 2006)
d: Numeraries are celibate Opus Dei members who live in the organisation's centres. Paola Binetti, a psychiatrist and professor at the Opus Dei-founded Campus Bio-Medico University in Rome, sat in the Italian parliament from 2006, latterly as a senator elected in 2018, for The Daisy, the Democratic Party and then the Union of the Centre. She has said publicly that she is a numerary and wears a cilice.
cite: Italian Senate member record; Binetti's own public statements

n: Kyriakos Mitsotakis — sitting Greek PM at Bilderberg 2025
d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, held under the Chatham House rule with no public record of what is said. The official list for the June 2025 meeting in Stockholm names Kyriakos Mitsotakis, who has been Greece's prime minister since 2019 and was in office at the time.
cite: Bilderberg Meetings official participant list, 71st meeting, Stockholm, 12–15 June 2025

n: Alexander Stubb — WEF Young Global Leader, now president
d: The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme picks about 100 people under 40 a year, including ministers and MPs, for a six-year network. The official CV published by the Office of the President of Finland lists Stubb as a 'Member of the Young Global Leader Network, World Economic Forum' (2009) and a member of the WEF Global Future Council on Europe (2018). He has been President of Finland since March 2024.
cite: Office of the President of the Republic of Finland, official curriculum vitae

n: Leo Varadkar — named WEF Young Global Leader while Taoiseach
d: The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme picks about 100 people under 40 a year for a six-year network. In May 2018 the WEF named sitting Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, then 39, in its 2018 class. Varadkar was also on the official Bilderberg list in 2024, weeks after stepping down as Taoiseach.

d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, held under the Chatham House rule with no public record of what is said. n: PwC partner shared Treasury tax plans with PwC colleagues
d: PwC is one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms that advise both governments and large companies. In 2013 the Treasury engaged PwC partner Peter Collins to advise on new laws against multinational tax avoidance; he shared confidential Treasury information with at least 53 PwC partners. The Tax Practitioners Board suspended his licence for two years in December 2022, and a Senate committee concluded PwC had followed a deliberate strategy over many years to cover up the breach. CEO Tom Seymour stepped down in May 2023, PwC removed eight partners, and in June 2023 sold its government consulting arm for $1 (now Scyne Advisory). Treasury referred the case to the Australian Federal Police in May 2023; police raided PwC's Sydney office in October 2024 and no charges have been reported.
cite: Senate Finance and Public Administration References Committee inquiry (2023); Tax Practitioners Board decision Dec 2022; AFP referral 24 May 2023

n: French Senate inquiry into consultants; McKinsey tax-fraud probe
d: McKinsey is a US management-consulting firm that sells advice to governments and companies. A French Senate commission of inquiry (chair Arnaud Bazin, rapporteur Eliane Assassi) reported in early 2022 that the state's use of consultants since 2017 was 'sprawling and opaque' and had real influence on policy, including during the Covid crisis; one example was a €496,800 McKinsey seminar for the Education Ministry. The Senate referred McKinsey's testimony on its French corporate tax to prosecutors in March 2022, and the National Financial Prosecutor (PNF) opened a money-laundering-of-tax-fraud investigation. On 4 September 2026 the PNF and Brussels prosecutors announced a €65 million seizure, about 96% of the tax loss they estimate; the investigation continues.
cite: French Senate commission of inquiry on consulting firms, report 2022; Parquet national financier statement 4 Sept 2026 (via Public Sénat)

n: McKinsey Africa admits bribing Eskom and Transnet officials
rank: state power and rail company officials
d: Eskom (electricity) and Transnet (ports and freight rail) are South Africa's largest state-owned companies. On 5 December 2024 McKinsey Africa entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, admitting a conspiracy to bribe officials at Eskom and Transnet for inside information on consulting contracts. It agreed to pay $122.85 million, part of it in South Africa; the Justice Department put McKinsey's profit from the scheme at about $85 million. Former senior partner Vikas Sagar pleaded guilty separately.
cite: US Department of Justice, deferred prosecution agreement, 5 Dec 2024 (Reuters via Daily Maverick)

n: Bain & Company and the takeover of the tax service (SARS)
d: Bain & Company is a US management-consulting firm. The Zondo Commission into state capture found in Part 1 of its report (4 January 2022) that President Jacob Zuma, SARS commissioner Tom Moyane and Bain worked together to take over the South African Revenue Service, whose powers to investigate organised crime were seen as a threat. An earlier commission under Judge Robert Nugent concluded that one Bain contract aimed to disable SARS. Bain says the allegations against it are unproven.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), Report Part 1, 4 Jan 2022; Nugent Commission of Inquiry into SARS, 2018

n: UK bars Bain from government contracts over SARS role
d: Bain & Company is a US consulting firm found by South Africa's Zondo Commission to have helped take over the country's tax service. In 2022 the UK government, after lobbying by Peter Hain, barred Bain from bidding for UK government contracts for three years. The ban was lifted in 2023, two years early, with the government saying Bain had cooperated and taken 'self-cleansing actions'. South Africa's government has also suspended Bain from state work.
cite: UK Cabinet Office procurement exclusion 2022, lifted 2023 (reported by Daily Maverick, 22 Jan 2025)

n: KPMG withdraws SARS 'rogue unit' report; nine executives resign
rank: South African Revenue Service; finance minister
d: KPMG is one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms. On 15 September 2017 KPMG South Africa withdrew all findings of its report on an alleged 'rogue unit' at the tax service SARS, a report that had fed criminal charges against former finance minister Pravin Gordhan, and apologised to him. KPMG International's review of the firm's audit work for Gupta family companies found risk checks had been skipped. CEO Trevor Hoole and eight other senior executives resigned, and KPMG offered to repay the R23 million SARS had paid for the report.
cite: KPMG South Africa / KPMG International statement, 15 Sept 2017 (Business Day)

n: Gupta family — finance ministry offered to deputy; Nene sacked
d: The Gupta brothers ran a business group (computers, media, mining) close to President Jacob Zuma. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked Finance Minister Nhlanhla Nene on 9 December 2015; he refused, and the Guptas deny it. The Zondo Commission found that ministers, senior ANC members and state-company heads acted corruptly to help the Guptas, named minister Malusi Gigaba, and said Nene's firing showed Zuma acted for the Gupta brothers. The US sanctioned the family in October 2019; the UAE later rejected South Africa's extradition request on a technicality.
cite: Public Protector, 'State of Capture' report, 2 Nov 2016; Zondo Commission reports 2022; US Treasury sanctions Oct 2019

n: Big Four staff seconded to Treasury to help write tax law
d: The Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC) lend staff to government departments. On 26 April 2013 the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee reported that the firms second staff to the Treasury to help draft tax legislation, and that on returning they can use that knowledge to advise clients on loopholes. Chair Margaret Hodge called it 'a ridiculous conflict of interest'. The committee recommended banning the practice; it noted the four firms employ almost 9,000 tax advisers.
cite: House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, 'Tax avoidance: the role of large accountancy firms', 26 Apr 2013 (Public Finance)

n: Uber Files — economy minister Macron helped Uber in France
d: The Uber Files are 124,000 internal Uber documents from 2013–2017, leaked by its former Europe lobbying chief Mark MacGann and published by The Guardian and partners on 10 July 2022. Texts with Uber chief Travis Kalanick suggest that Emmanuel Macron, then economy minister (2014–16), brokered a secret deal with Uber's opponents in the cabinet. When police in Marseille banned an Uber service, Macron's office was contacted and the ban was lifted two days later. Macron said he was proud of supporting the company.
cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, 'The Uber Files', 10 July 2022

n: Uber Files — ex-EU commissioner Kroes lobbied Dutch officials
d: Neelie Kroes was EU digital commissioner until 2014. The leaked Uber Files (July 2022) show her helping Uber lobby Dutch politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Rutte, during her 18-month cooling-off period, after Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker refused her request to work for Uber formally. She denies wrongdoing.
cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, 'The Uber Files', July 2022

n: Pfizergate — von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's CEO
d: In 2021 Commission President Ursula von der Leyen negotiated the EU's largest vaccine contract (up to 1.8 billion doses) partly by text message with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla. The Commission refused to release the texts; the European Ombudsman found maladministration in July 2022. On 14 May 2025 the Grand Chamber of the EU General Court annulled the refusal in a case brought by The New York Times, holding that EU bodies must keep such documents or explain plausibly why they cannot; the Commission did not appeal. The European Public Prosecutor's Office confirmed an investigation into the vaccine purchases in October 2022.
cite: European Ombudsman decision, 12 July 2022; EU General Court (Grand Chamber), New York Times v Commission, 14 May 2025

n: Greensill Capital — Cameron texts Chancellor Sunak for access
rank: Chancellor of the Exchequer; Cabinet Office
d: Greensill Capital was a supply-chain finance firm that collapsed in March 2021. Lex Greensill had earlier held a Cabinet Office adviser role, which the Boardman review said gave him 'extraordinarily privileged' access to Downing Street; former Prime Minister David Cameron, later paid by Greensill, texted Chancellor Rishi Sunak in 2020 asking for the firm to join a Covid lending scheme, which Sunak declined. The Treasury Committee (20 July 2021) and the Boardman review (21 July 2021) found Cameron broke no rules but called the rules too weak. The government's former chief commercial officer Bill Crothers advised Greensill while still a civil servant.
cite: House of Commons Treasury Committee report, 20 July 2021; Boardman review for the Cabinet Office, 21 July 2021

n: SNC-Lavalin — ethics commissioner finds Trudeau broke conflict law
d: SNC-Lavalin (now AtkinsRéalis) is a Montreal engineering company that faced bribery charges over Libya. It lobbied for a law allowing deferred prosecution deals, with 51 meetings with officials and MPs over about 20 months. On 14 August 2019 Ethics Commissioner Mario Dion found Prime Minister Justin Trudeau broke section 9 of the Conflict of Interest Act by pressing Attorney General Jody Wilson-Raybould to overrule prosecutors, who had refused SNC a deal. The company later pleaded guilty to fraud and was fined C$280 million (December 2019).
cite: Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner, 'Trudeau II Report', 14 Aug 2019

n: John Dalli — EU health commissioner out after snus bribe request
d: Swedish Match is a Swedish maker of snus, an oral tobacco banned for sale in most of the EU. The EU anti-fraud office OLAF reported in October 2012 that a Maltese associate of Health Commissioner John Dalli asked Swedish Match for €60 million in return for help with EU tobacco rules; it found no money changed hands but concluded Dalli knew of the approach. Commission President José Manuel Barroso required Dalli to leave on 16 October 2012. The EU General Court dismissed Dalli's challenge in May 2015.
cite: OLAF report, Oct 2012; EU General Court, Case T-562/12 Dalli v Commission, 12 May 2015

n: Barroso — ex-Commission president becomes Goldman Sachs chairman
rank: former President of the European Commission
d: Goldman Sachs is a US investment bank. In July 2016, about two months after his 18-month cooling-off period ended, José Manuel Barroso (Commission president 2004–14) became non-executive chairman of Goldman Sachs International. His successor Jean-Claude Juncker ordered an unprecedented ethics review; in October 2016 the ethics committee found 'not sufficient grounds' for a breach, accepting Barroso's assurance that he would not lobby for the bank.
cite: European Commission ad hoc Ethical Committee opinion, Oct 2016

n: Qatargate — European Parliament vice-president and an NGO conduit
rank: Vice-President of the European Parliament; MEPs
d: Fight Impunity was a Brussels human-rights NGO led by former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri. Belgian police raided homes and offices on 9 December 2022 and seized about €1.5 million in cash; prosecutors allege Qatar and Morocco paid to influence Parliament, with money passing through the NGO. Vice-President Eva Kaili was removed from that post and charged; MEPs Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino were arrested in February 2023 and ex-MEP Marie Arena was charged in 2025. Panzeri took a plea deal in January 2023; the others deny wrongdoing, and in February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the prosecution could go ahead.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor; Brussels Court of Appeal ruling Feb 2026

n: Huawei bribery probe — Parliament lifts Italian MEP's immunity
d: Huawei is a Chinese telecoms-equipment maker. In March 2025 Belgian police searched Huawei's Brussels office and Parliament premises; prosecutors allege associates of former Huawei lobbyist Valerio Ottati paid MEPs to sign a 2021 letter opposing curbs on foreign 5G equipment, with up to €15,000 for the author and €1,500 per co-signer. Five people have been charged. On 16 June 2026 Parliament voted 344–234 to lift the immunity of Italian EPP MEP Fulvio Martusciello, who denies wrongdoing, while keeping immunity for three other MEPs.
cite: Belgian federal prosecutor; European Parliament plenary vote 16 June 2026 (Euronews)

n: Huawei Poland executive and ex-security-service officer tried for spying
d: Polish authorities arrested Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee in Poland, and Piotr Durbajło, a cybersecurity expert who had worked for state agencies including the Internal Security Agency, in January 2019. Prosecutors charged both with working for Chinese intelligence; they say Wang sought contracts from 2011 to 2019 that would give Huawei insight into state and local government data systems. Both pleaded not guilty; the trial opened in Warsaw in June 2021 and was closed to the public.
cite: Polish prosecutors' indictment; Warsaw district court trial from June 2021 (AP via Courthouse News)

n: African Union headquarters — data sent to Shanghai every night
d: China built and paid for the roughly $200 million African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, opened in 2012, and Huawei supplied most of its computer and network equipment. Le Monde reported on 26 January 2018 that from 2012 to January 2017 the building's data were copied each night to servers in Shanghai, and that bugs were found in desks and walls. The AU replaced its servers and declined Chinese offers to set them up. China called the report 'ridiculous', and Huawei said its equipment was not the source; no public evidence of a backdoor has been shown.
cite: Le Monde, 26 Jan 2018 (summarised by New America)

n: Cambridge Analytica ran Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns
d: Cambridge Analytica was a British political-data firm that closed in 2018. In an undercover Channel 4 recording broadcast in March 2018, managing director Mark Turnbull said the firm ran Uhuru Kenyatta's campaigns in 2013 and 2017, 'rebranded the party twice' and wrote its manifesto. The company then confirmed it was behind the TNA and Jubilee presidential campaigns.
cite: Channel 4 News undercover investigation, 19 Mar 2018; company confirmation (The Star, Kenya)

n: Alejandro Toledo — 20 years for Odebrecht highway bribes
d: Odebrecht is a Brazilian construction group that in 2016 admitted to US authorities paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries through a dedicated bribery department. Former president Alejandro Toledo was extradited from the United States on 23 April 2023. On 21 October 2024 a Lima court sentenced him to 20 years for taking about $35 million from Odebrecht in return for the Interoceanic Highway contract.
cite: Peru, National Superior Court of Specialized Criminal Justice, 21 Oct 2024

n: Ollanta Humala and Nadine Heredia — 15 years in Odebrecht case
d: Odebrecht is the Brazilian construction group at the centre of Latin America's largest bribery case. On 15 April 2025 a Lima court convicted former president Ollanta Humala and his wife Nadine Heredia of money laundering linked to Odebrecht and sentenced each to 15 years; prosecutors had argued Odebrecht and the Venezuelan government financed his 2006 and 2011 campaigns. Heredia left for Brasília after Brazil granted her diplomatic asylum. Both deny the charges.
