cite: Peru, National Superior Court of Specialized Criminal Justice, 15 Apr 2025

n: Jorge Glas — vice-president jailed for $13.5m Odebrecht bribes
d: Odebrecht is a Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America. On 15 December 2017 Vice-President Jorge Glas was sentenced to six years for taking about $13.5 million from Odebrecht; the National Court of Justice upheld it in October 2019. He received further sentences in 2020, 2021 and 2025, was seized by police inside Mexico's embassy in Quito on 5 April 2024, and was moved to a maximum-security prison in November 2025.
cite: Ecuador, National Court of Justice, sentence 15 Dec 2017, upheld Oct 2019

n: Emilio Lozoya — ex-Pemex chief extradited over Odebrecht bribes
d: Pemex is Mexico's state oil company. Emilio Lozoya ran it from December 2012 to February 2016 and is accused of taking about $10 million in bribes from the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht. Spanish police arrested him in Málaga in February 2020 and he was extradited to Mexico on 17 July 2020. He denies the charges; in February 2024 he was moved from prison to house arrest, and no verdict has been reported.
cite: Mexico, Fiscalía General de la República charges; extradition 17 July 2020

n: Lula's Car Wash convictions annulled
d: Operation Car Wash (2014–21) investigated a cartel of construction firms, Odebrecht among them, that paid politicians for contracts with the state oil company Petrobras; it charged 429 people. Former president Lula da Silva was convicted in July 2017 (a beachfront apartment) and February 2019 (a family country house) and jailed in April 2018. On 8 March 2021 Supreme Court justice Edson Fachin annulled both convictions because the Curitiba court of judge Sergio Moro lacked jurisdiction, restoring Lula's political rights; in 2023 Justice Dias Toffoli voided evidence from Odebrecht's leniency deal.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, Justice Edson Fachin ruling, 8 Mar 2021

n: Manuel Chang — ex-finance minister convicted over 'tuna bonds'
d: Privinvest is an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group. About $2 billion in loans arranged by Credit Suisse and others went to three Mozambican state companies for fishing and maritime security, partly hidden from the IMF. A Brooklyn jury convicted former finance minister Manuel Chang in August 2024 of wire-fraud and money-laundering conspiracy; prosecutors said Privinvest paid him $7 million. He was sentenced to eight and a half years on 17 January 2025. Credit Suisse paid about $475 million in 2021, and London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from Privinvest's owner's estate.
cite: US District Court (E.D.N.Y.), verdict Aug 2024, sentence 17 Jan 2025; UK High Court judgment 2024

n: Najib Razak — 1MDB conviction; Goldman bankers moved the money
d: 1MDB was a Malaysian state investment fund. Goldman Sachs bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged its bond deals with financier Jho Low; US authorities say money was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the UAE. Goldman settled with Malaysia in July 2020 for about $3.9 billion; Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York in 2022. On 26 December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found former prime minister Najib Razak guilty on all 25 counts tied to over $1 billion in his personal accounts and sentenced him to 15 years; he is appealing.
cite: High Court of Malaysia, 26 Dec 2025; US v. Roger Ng (E.D.N.Y.) 2022; Goldman–Malaysia settlement July 2020

n: Glencore admits bribery in Nigeria and four other African states
d: Glencore is a Swiss-based commodity trader. In May 2022 it pleaded guilty in the United States to bribing officials in several countries from 2007 to 2018 and agreed to pay over $1 billion. In June 2022 its UK subsidiary pleaded guilty to seven counts of bribery; the Serious Fraud Office found more than $28 million in bribes paid in Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan between 2012 and 2016.
cite: US Department of Justice plea, May 2022; UK Serious Fraud Office, Southwark Crown Court plea, 21 June 2022

n: Glencore pays Congo $180m over bribery of officials
d: Glencore is a Swiss-based commodity trader and one of the largest mining firms in the Democratic Republic of Congo. US authorities said it paid $27.5 million to third parties from 2007 to 2018 intending part to bribe Congolese officials. In December 2022 Glencore agreed to pay Congo $180 million to settle the claims.
cite: Glencore–DR Congo settlement, Dec 2022; US Department of Justice plea, May 2022

n: Gunvor — $661m over corruption in Ecuador
d: Gunvor is a Geneva-based oil trader. In March 2024 it resolved US and Swiss investigations into its past business in Ecuador, paying about $374 million in fines and $287 million in forfeiture, and the Swiss Attorney General convicted it of corruption in Ecuador. In 2019 Swiss authorities had already penalised it about $95 million for failing to prevent bribery of officials in Côte d'Ivoire and the Republic of Congo.
cite: US Department of Justice resolution and Swiss Office of the Attorney General summary penalty order, March 2024

n: Trafigura convicted in Switzerland for bribing an Angolan official
rank: official at a Sonangol (state oil) subsidiary
d: Trafigura is one of the world's largest oil and metals traders. In January 2025 the Swiss Federal Criminal Court convicted it and former chief operating officer Mike Wainwright over €4.3 million in bribes paid in 2009–11 to an Angolan official linked to a subsidiary of Sonangol, Angola's state oil company. Trafigura was fined $3.3 million and ordered to pay $145.6 million; Wainwright got 32 months, 20 suspended. Trafigura has appealed, so the ruling is not yet final.
cite: Swiss Federal Criminal Court, Bellinzona, Jan 2025

n: Trafigura pleads guilty to bribing Petrobras officials
d: Trafigura is a commodity trader. On 28 March 2024 it pleaded guilty in the United States to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act by bribing Brazilian officials at Petrobras from 2003 to 2014, paying up to 20 cents per barrel through shell companies. It agreed to pay about $127 million.
cite: US Department of Justice plea agreement, 28 Mar 2024

n: Adani indicted in New York over bribes to Indian officials
d: The Adani Group is an Indian conglomerate in ports, power and airports. On 20 November 2024 US federal prosecutors in New York charged founder Gautam Adani and associates with fraud, alleging more than $250 million in bribes to Indian government officials for solar power contracts. Adani denies the charges. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's civil case is ongoing; in January 2026 it asked an Indian court to serve summonses by email.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, indictment 20 Nov 2024; SEC civil complaint

n: Kenya cancels Adani airport and power deals after US charges
d: The Adani Group, an Indian conglomerate, had proposed to lease Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and to build power lines. A day after Adani's directors were charged with bribery in New York in November 2024, President William Ruto cancelled both deals.
cite: Statement by President William Ruto, Nov 2024

n: Larry Householder — Ohio Speaker, 20 years over FirstEnergy money
rank: Speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives
d: FirstEnergy is an Ohio power company. Prosecutors showed it funnelled about $60 million to a group around House Speaker Larry Householder in return for House Bill 6, a $1 billion-plus rescue of its nuclear plants. A jury convicted Householder of racketeering on 9 March 2023 and he was sentenced to 20 years on 29 June 2023. FirstEnergy agreed in July 2021 to pay a $230 million penalty.
cite: US District Court (S.D. Ohio), verdict 9 Mar 2023, sentence 29 June 2023

n: Michael Madigan — Illinois Speaker convicted in ComEd bribery
rank: Speaker of the Illinois House of Representatives
d: Commonwealth Edison (ComEd) is Chicago's electricity utility. Prosecutors showed it gave jobs and contracts to associates of House Speaker Michael Madigan, the longest-serving legislative leader in US history, to win support for its bills. A federal jury convicted him on 12 February 2025 of 10 counts including bribery and conspiracy; he was sentenced to 7½ years and a $2.5 million fine and began serving in October 2025. The 7th Circuit upheld the conviction on 27 April 2026.
cite: US District Court (N.D. Ill.), verdict 12 Feb 2025; US Court of Appeals, 7th Circuit, 27 Apr 2026

n: Pharmally — Duterte adviser and ₱8.68bn pandemic contracts
rank: head of the Budget Department's Procurement Service
d: Pharmally Pharmaceutical was founded in 2019 with ₱625,000 in paid-up capital and won nine pandemic supply contracts worth ₱8.68 billion. Its chairman told senators that Michael Yang, a former presidential adviser to Rodrigo Duterte, acted as financier and guarantor for its Chinese suppliers; Yang denies formal ties. A Senate Blue Ribbon draft report signed by nine senators recommended charges. In May 2024 the Ombudsman ordered graft charges against procurement chief Lloyd Christopher Lao and ex-health secretary Francisco Duque III, and the anti-graft court issued Lao's arrest warrant in September 2024.
cite: Senate Blue Ribbon Committee partial report, 2022; Office of the Ombudsman, May 2024; Sandiganbayan, Sept 2024

n: Gerhard Schröder — ex-chancellor on Russian state energy boards
d: Rosneft and Gazprom are Russian state-controlled energy companies; Nord Stream built the gas pipelines under the Baltic. Gerhard Schröder, chancellor until 2005, became chairman of the Nord Stream shareholders' committee in 2006 and joined Rosneft's board in 2017, later chairing it; he gave up the chairmanship in 2022 and turned down a Gazprom board seat that year. In 2022 the Bundestag closed his ex-chancellor's office; Berlin courts rejected his challenges in 2023 and 2024. An SPD arbitration panel ruled in March 2023 that he could stay in the party.
cite: Bundestag decision 2022; Berlin administrative courts 2023 and 2024

n: Karin Kneissl — ex-foreign minister on Rosneft's board
d: Rosneft is Russia's state oil company. Karin Kneissl was Austria's foreign minister from December 2017 to June 2019, nominated by the FPÖ; Vladimir Putin attended her wedding in August 2018. In March 2021 the Russian government appointed her to Rosneft's board; she resigned in May 2022. She moved to Russia in 2023 and works at a research centre at St Petersburg State University.
cite: Rosneft board appointment, March 2021 (Reuters and others)

n: Gates Foundation — second-largest funder of the WHO
d: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation is a private US charity. In 2020 it was the World Health Organization's second-largest contributor; in the period cited it gave 45% of the WHO's funds from non-state bodies, about 12% of WHO operating spending. Most of this money is earmarked for the foundation's chosen programmes. Academics and charities have warned this can tilt WHO priorities toward the foundation's own.
cite: WHO contributor data as summarised by Wikipedia

n: Kristalina Georgieva — Doing Business data changed for China
rank: World Bank CEO; IMF Managing Director
d: The World Bank's annual Doing Business report ranked countries' business rules and shaped investment and reform decisions. In September 2021 an inquiry by the law firm WilmerHale found that Kristalina Georgieva, as World Bank chief executive, had pressed staff to alter data in the 2018 report to raise China's (and Saudi Arabia's) ranking. She denied it; the IMF board, where she was Managing Director, said the evidence did not conclusively show wrongdoing and kept her. The IMF reappointed her for a second five-year term on 12 April 2024.
cite: WilmerHale investigation for the World Bank Board, Sept 2021; IMF Executive Board statement, Oct 2021

n: Reza Baqir — IMF official named central bank governor
rank: Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan
d: The IMF lends to countries in crisis on condition of policy changes. Reza Baqir, an IMF staff member who had been mission chief for Romania and Bulgaria, was appointed Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan on 4 May 2019, a day after his predecessor was abruptly removed, while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout (Reuters). He served until 4 May 2022.
cite: Government of Pakistan appointment, 4 May 2019 (Reuters)

n: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala — World Bank chief to finance minister
rank: Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy
d: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala was a World Bank managing director from December 2007 to 2011, after a 25-year career there. President Goodluck Jonathan appointed her finance minister and coordinating minister for the economy on 17 August 2011, a post she held until May 2015. She became Director-General of the World Trade Organization in March 2021 and was reappointed in November 2024.
cite: Nigerian presidential appointment, 17 Aug 2011; WTO General Council decisions 2021 and 2024

n: Interpol curbs Russia's direct use of its channels
d: Interpol lets national police forces send each other wanted-person alerts. On 10 March 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, Interpol's General Secretariat stopped Russia's bureau from sending alerts ('diffusions') directly to other countries; each must first be checked against Interpol's rules. The Secretary General also put Russia under enhanced supervision, endorsed by the Executive Committee, to prevent misuse against individuals.
cite: INTERPOL General Secretariat statement, 10 Mar 2022

n: French terror prosecutors open torture inquiry into Interpol president
rank: UAE Interior Ministry inspector general; Interpol president
d: Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, a senior UAE Interior Ministry officer, was Interpol's president from November 2021 to November 2025. Complaints were filed in Paris alleging torture of activist Ahmed Mansoor and of Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad in UAE custody. In March 2022 France's anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry into torture and acts of barbarism, and Hedges and Ahmad testified before Paris investigating judges in May 2022. Al-Raisi denies the allegations.
cite: Parquet national antiterroriste (France), preliminary inquiry opened March 2022

n: ICAO — 2016 hack by China-linked group and internal cover-up
d: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is the UN agency that sets world aviation standards. CBC reported in February 2019, from internal documents, that a November 2016 cyberattack most likely by Emissary Panda, a group tied to the Chinese government, used ICAO's systems to infect visitors, and that ICT staff and their supervisor tried to hide evidence; sources said Secretary General Fang Liu, a Chinese national, shelved recommendations to investigate them. ICAO disputed the account. The US ambassador to ICAO later called the handling 'unacceptable'.
cite: CBC News investigation, Feb 2019

n: Wu Hongbo — UN official says he had Uyghur leader removed
rank: UN Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs
d: Wu Hongbo, a Chinese diplomat, headed the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs from 2012 to 2017. On China's CCTV in December 2018 he said that in 2017 he had UN security remove Dolkun Isa, president of the World Uyghur Congress, from the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and that as a Chinese international civil servant he 'firmly defends the motherland's interests'. UN staff rules require officials not to take instructions from any government.
cite: CCTV programme 'Kaijiang La', Dec 2018 (transcript via China Digital Times)

n: Qu Dongyu — Chinese vice-minister elected head of FAO
rank: Director-General of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization
d: The FAO is the UN's food and farming agency, based in Rome. Qu Dongyu, China's vice-minister of agriculture (2015–19), won its top post on 23 June 2019 with 108 of 191 votes, ahead of the EU-backed French candidate; allegations of Chinese pressure and inducements on voting delegations featured in the election. A 2023 study by German public broadcasters found he had used the FAO for Beijing's interests. He remains Director-General.
cite: 41st FAO Conference vote, 23 June 2019; German public broadcasters' investigation 2023

n: Ng Lap Seng — Macau tycoon convicted of bribing UN Assembly president
rank: President of the UN General Assembly
d: Ng Lap Seng is a Macau property developer. A Manhattan federal jury convicted him in July 2017 of paying about $500,000 in bribes to John Ashe, President of the UN General Assembly and Antigua's UN ambassador, and paying Dominican Republic deputy ambassador Francis Lorenzo, to win UN backing for a conference centre in Macau. He was sentenced to four years in May 2018.
cite: US District Court (S.D.N.Y.), verdict July 2017, sentence May 2018

n: Michael Lauber — Swiss attorney general out over secret FIFA meetings
d: FIFA, world football's governing body, is based in Zurich, and Switzerland's federal prosecutors were investigating FIFA corruption. Attorney General Michael Lauber met FIFA president Gianni Infantino in 2016 and 2017 without keeping records. Lauber was found to have misled the body that oversees federal prosecutors and left office in 2020. A special prosecutor opened a criminal case against Infantino over the meetings; it was closed without charges on 26 October 2023.
cite: Swiss Federal Administrative Court ruling 2020; Swiss special prosecutor decision, 26 Oct 2023 (AP)

n: Haruyuki Takahashi — Tokyo 2020 board member charged with bribery
rank: board member, Tokyo 2020 Olympic organising committee
d: The Tokyo 2020 organising committee ran the Olympics under the IOC and counted as a public body under Japanese law. Haruyuki Takahashi, a board member and former executive of the ad agency Dentsu, was arrested in 2022 and charged with taking about ¥198 million (about $1.4 million) from sponsors and licensees including Aoki Holdings and Kadokawa. About a dozen people on the paying side were convicted, all with suspended sentences. Takahashi pleaded not guilty and his trial opened in Tokyo District Court.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors indictment 2022; Tokyo District Court trial 2023–24 (AP)

n: CICIG — UN-backed commission's case ends Pérez Molina presidency
d: CICIG was an international commission set up by a 2006 UN–Guatemala agreement to help Guatemala's prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state. In 2015 CICIG and the Public Ministry exposed 'La Línea', a customs-bribery ring reaching Vice-President Roxana Baldetti and President Otto Pérez Molina. Congress lifted his immunity 132–0 and he resigned on 2 September 2015. On 7 December 2022 both were sentenced to 16 years; Pérez Molina was released on bond in January 2024.
cite: Guatemala, Sentencing Court, 7 Dec 2022; Congress vote 1 Sept 2015

n: Jimmy Morales ends CICIG while under its investigation
d: CICIG, the UN-backed anti-impunity commission, was investigating irregular financing of President Jimmy Morales's campaign. In 2018 Morales said he would not renew its mandate and deployed armed forces near its offices; on 7 January 2019 he terminated the agreement. The UN rejected the move and the Constitutional Court ruled against it, but CICIG's mandate ended on 3 September 2019.
cite: Government of Guatemala notice, 7 Jan 2019; Constitutional Court rulings 2019

n: Tony Blair Institute — strategy units inside Rwanda's government
rank: Office of the President / Prime Minister (strategy and delivery units)
d: The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change is a London-based non-profit that places advisers inside governments; it reports work with governments in more than 45 countries and had about 1,000 staff in 2026. In Rwanda it has supported a Strategy and Policy Unit and a Government Action Coordination Unit and worked on the Imihigo performance-contract system; in Kenya it supported a Presidential Delivery Unit. Its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation, which gave over £52 million in 2023 (The Guardian).
cite: Tony Blair Institute published programme descriptions; The Guardian, Apr 2025

n: Erik Prince — UN panel finds he broke the Libya arms embargo
d: Erik Prince founded the US private military company Blackwater. A UN Panel of Experts report in February 2021 found he violated the UN arms embargo on Libya in a 2019 operation to supply aircraft and personnel to forces of eastern commander Khalifa Haftar; the planned $80 million deal collapsed in June 2019. Prince denies wrongdoing.
cite: UN Security Council Panel of Experts on Libya, report Feb 2021

n: Erik Prince — security deal with Ecuador's President Noboa
d: Erik Prince founded Blackwater and now runs other private security ventures. In March 2025 he and President Daniel Noboa announced a deal for Prince to support Ecuador's security forces against gangs.
cite: Joint announcement by President Noboa and Erik Prince, March 2025

n: Vectus Global — Prince's contractors in Haiti's anti-gang raids
d: Vectus Global is a private security company run by Erik Prince, founder of Blackwater. Reuters reported in August 2025 that Prince planned to keep personnel in Haiti for ten years to fight gangs and help collect taxes. In January 2026 Haitian authorities confirmed Vectus took part in anti-gang raids.
cite: Reuters, Aug 2025; Haitian authorities' confirmation, Jan 2026

n: Erik Prince sends men and drones to help Congo's army
rank: Armed Forces of the DR Congo (FARDC)
d: Erik Prince founded Blackwater. A UN report in 2023 described a proposed Prince mercenary deal for North Kivu, and in February 2026 Reuters reported that Prince sent men and drones to help Congo's army secure the eastern city of Uvira.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the DR Congo, 2023; Reuters, Feb 2026

n: Ulf Kristersson — Prime Minister addresses Bilderberg in Stockholm
d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private, off-the-record annual conference of about 120 European and North American political, business and military figures. It met at the Grand Hôtel, Stockholm, on 12–15 June 2025; Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson attended and was scheduled to speak on Swedish and EU competitiveness and support for Ukraine, though he was not on the published list. Topics included transatlantic relations, Ukraine, critical raw materials and AI.
cite: Bilderberg Meetings participant list 2025; RTÉ / Reuters, 12 June 2025

arch.t: Bilderberg Group — Coordinated Policy-Making Before Public Positions Adopted

n: Serving US officials and commanders at Bilderberg 2025
rank: White House science director; regional military commanders; House committee chair
d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private annual conference of Western political, business and military figures. The published list for the June 2025 meeting in Stockholm included White House science and technology director Michael Kratsios, Admiral Samuel Paparo (commander, US Indo-Pacific Command), General Christopher Donahue (commander, US Army Europe and Africa) and Representative Jason Smith (chair of the House Ways and Means Committee), alongside executives such as Palantir's Alex Karp and Pfizer's Albert Bourla.
cite: Bilderberg Meetings participant list 2025

arch.t: Bilderberg Group — Coordinated Policy-Making Before Public Positions Adopted

n: Mark Rutte — NATO Secretary General at Bilderberg 2025
d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private annual conference of Western political, business and military figures. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Dutch prime minister from 2010 to 2024, attended the June 2025 meeting in Stockholm, where Ukraine and transatlantic relations were on the agenda.
cite: Bilderberg Meetings participant list 2025; RTÉ / Reuters, 12 June 2025

arch.t: Bilderberg Group — Coordinated Policy-Making Before Public Positions Adopted

n: Alexander Stubb — President of Finland, WEF Young Global Leader
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Alexander Stubb, a former prime minister and finance minister, is listed among its alumni. He has been President of Finland since 1 March 2024.
cite: Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders (WEF alumni)

n: King Frederik X — WEF Young Global Leader on Denmark's throne
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Frederik, then crown prince, is listed among its alumni. He became King of Denmark in January 2024.
cite: Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders (WEF alumni)

n: King Willem-Alexander — WEF Young Global Leader alumnus
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Willem-Alexander, then Prince of Orange, is listed among its alumni. He has been King of the Netherlands since 2013.
cite: Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders (WEF alumni)

n: Ruben Brekelmans — Dutch defence minister in YGL class of 2025
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 (116 people) included Ruben Brekelmans, then Minister of Defence of the Netherlands.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Mélanie Joly — Canadian minister and WEF Young Global Leader
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Mélanie Joly is a member of the programme, as noted by the City of Münster when she attended the 2022 G7 foreign ministers' meeting as Canada's foreign minister. She has been Minister of Industry since 13 May 2025.
cite: City of Münster G7 guest profiles, 2022; Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders

n: Annalena Baerbock — Germany's foreign minister, WEF Young Global Leader
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Annalena Baerbock is a member of the programme, as noted by the City of Münster when she hosted the 2022 G7 foreign ministers' meeting. She was Germany's foreign minister from December 2021 to May 2025 and in 2025 became President of the UN General Assembly.
cite: City of Münster G7 guest profiles, 2022; Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders

n: Ram Mohan Naidu — India's aviation minister in YGL class of 2025
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu, India's Minister of Civil Aviation since June 2024.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Simon Harris — Tánaiste named to YGL class of 2025
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Simon Harris, Ireland's former Taoiseach, then Tánaiste, foreign minister and defence minister.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Paetongtarn Shinawatra — named YGL while Thai prime minister
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Paetongtarn Shinawatra while she was Prime Minister of Thailand. The Constitutional Court removed her from office in August 2025.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Milojko Spajić — named YGL while Montenegro's prime minister
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Milojko Spajić, Prime Minister of Montenegro.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Siviwe Gwarube — South Africa's education minister in YGL 2025
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Siviwe Gwarube, South Africa's Minister of Basic Education.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Timčo Mucunski — North Macedonia's foreign minister in YGL 2025
rank: Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Timčo Mucunski, North Macedonia's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Erkki Keldo — Estonia's economy minister in YGL 2025
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Erkki Keldo, Estonia's Minister of Economy and Industry.
cite: World Economic Forum, 'Meet the YGL class of 2025'

n: Vera Daves — Angola's finance minister, WEF Young Global Leader
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Vera Daves de Sousa is listed among its alumni. She has been Angola's Minister of Finance since 8 October 2019.
cite: Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders (WEF alumni)

n: Anielle Franco — Brazil's racial equality minister, YGL 2024
d: The World Economic Forum (the Davos forum) picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Anielle Franco, Brazil's Minister of Racial Equality in the Lula government, was selected in 2024.
cite: Wikipedia list of Young Global Leaders (WEF alumni)

n: Evangelical Parliamentary Front — 213 deputies and 26 senators
rank: organised caucus in both houses of Congress
d: The Frente Parlamentar Evangélica is a registered cross-party caucus of Protestant, mostly Pentecostal, members of Brazil's National Congress. It was formally registered with the Chamber of Deputies in 2015, after the 2002 election brought in 60 deputies who declared themselves evangelical. Its registered membership in the current legislature is 213 of 513 deputies and 26 of 81 senators. A few members sit on the left, such as Benedita da Silva and Marina Silva; most vote with the conservative bloc.
cite: Chamber of Deputies register 'Frentes e Grupos Parlamentares' (May 2023), via Wikipedia; Folha de S.Paulo, 5 Feb 2025

n: Republicanos — party founded by Universal Church pastors
rank: party president and vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies
d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG) is a Brazilian neo-Pentecostal church founded by Bishop Edir Macedo in 1977. Its pastors founded the party now called Republicanos in August 2005. The party's president since 2018, Marcos Pereira, is a UCKG bishop; he was Minister of Industry and Foreign Trade in 2016–18 and has been a vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies since 2019. Political scientist David Fleischer called it 'an evangelical party', though many of its members are Catholic.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Republicanos', citing Fleischer and party records

n: Marcelo Crivella — Universal Church bishop as minister and Rio mayor
rank: federal minister, senator and mayor of Rio de Janeiro
d: Crivella is a bishop of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God and the nephew of its founder, Edir Macedo. He was a senator for Rio de Janeiro from 2003 to 2016, Minister of Fishing and Aquaculture under Dilma Rousseff in 2012–14, and mayor of Rio from 2017 to 2020. He was arrested on 22 December 2020, days before his term ended, in a corruption investigation.
cite: The Guardian, 22 Dec 2020; Wikipedia biography

n: Milton Ribeiro — pastor-minister and the pastors' education-fund scheme
d: Ribeiro is a Presbyterian pastor from Santos whom Jair Bolsonaro made education minister in July 2020. A leaked audio in March 2022 pointed to a scheme in which two pastors without government posts steered money from the National Education Development Fund (FNDE) to towns, allegedly in exchange for bribes. Ribeiro left office on 28 March 2022. The Federal Police arrested him on 22 June 2022 on a warrant citing passive corruption, malfeasance and influence peddling.
cite: G1, 10 Jul 2020; Federal Police arrest warrant, 22 Jun 2022, via Wikipedia

n: André Mendonça — Presbyterian pastor on the Supreme Court
rank: Justice of the Supreme Federal Court
d: Mendonça is a pastor of the Presbyterian Church of Brazil who served Bolsonaro as Attorney General of the Union and Minister of Justice. Bolsonaro, who had said he wanted an evangelical on the court, named him to the Supreme Federal Court; the Senate confirmed him 47–32 on 1 December 2021. He sits on the court today.
cite: Bloomberg, 12 Jul 2021; Senate vote, 1 Dec 2021, via Wikipedia

n: Damares Alves — pastor, human rights minister, now senator
rank: Minister of Women, Families and Human Rights; senator
d: Alves is an evangelical pastor who served in the Foursquare Gospel Church and the Lagoinha Baptist Church. Bolsonaro made her Minister of Women, Families and Human Rights from January 2019 to March 2022. She was elected senator for the Federal District in 2022 for Republicanos and took her seat in February 2023.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Brazilian press

n: Brazil's Congress holds session for Grande Oriente bicentenary
rank: joint session of the National Congress
d: The Grande Oriente do Brasil is the country's oldest Masonic body. On 17 June 2022 the National Congress held a special session to mark its 200 years, requested by Senator Izalci Lucas (PSDB-DF) and Deputy General Girão (PL-RN), both described by the Senate's radio service as Masons. Grand Master Múcio Bonifácio Guimarães spoke, with lodge delegates from 14 countries present.
cite: Rádio Senado, 20 Jun 2022

n: Angola removes Universal Church's Brazilian leadership
rank: government order dissolving the church's board
d: The Brazilian-run Universal Church of the Kingdom of God built a large following in Angola. After Angolan pastors accused Brazilian leaders of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the Angolan government in June 2020 ordered the dissolution of the church's board and removed Bishop Honorilton Gonçalves. The church had already been suspended for 60 days in 2013 after a deadly crush at a Luanda stadium event.
cite: Angolan government order, June 2020, via Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God'

n: William Ruto — plan for an 8,000-seat church at State House
d: Ruto is an evangelical Christian who led a church choir of the Africa Inland Church and married in that church. In July 2025 he announced he would build a church in the State House grounds with his own money. The Daily Nation published designs for a building seating 8,000 people at an expected cost of about $9 million; Nairobi's Catholic archbishop and the Atheists in Kenya Society objected that it breached the secular state.
cite: Daily Nation, July 2025, via Wikipedia 'William Ruto'

n: Patrick Njoroge — Opus Dei numerary as central bank governor
rank: Governor of the Central Bank of Kenya
d: Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation whose celibate 'numerary' members live in its centres. Njoroge, a numerary, was nominated by President Uhuru Kenyatta and approved by Parliament in June 2015, and governed the Central Bank of Kenya until June 2023. He also sat ex officio on the IMF Board of Governors. His brother Anthony Muheria is Catholic archbishop of Nyeri.
cite: Parliament of Kenya approval, 18 Jun 2015; Wikipedia biography and 'List of members of Opus Dei'

n: David Bahati — Fellowship prayer-breakfast chair in Uganda's cabinet
rank: Minister of State for Trade, Industry and Cooperatives
d: The Fellowship (also called The Family) is a US Christian network that runs national prayer breakfasts for politicians. Bahati chairs Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast Fellowship. Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that Bahati first floated his 2009 Anti-Homosexuality Bill, which proposed the death penalty, at the 2008 Uganda prayer breakfast; Fellowship member Bob Hunter confirmed Bahati's link to NPR. Bahati has been a state minister since 2021 and was re-appointed in 2026.
cite: Jeff Sharlet reporting; NPR, Dec 2009; Wikipedia biography

n: Uganda's 2023 anti-gay law and Family Watch International
d: Family Watch International is an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group with UN consultative status and a strong presence in Africa. Uganda passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023, with life imprisonment and, in some cases, death. A Ugandan activist named FWI president Sharon Slater as having lobbied for the law; FWI earlier described its position on the 2009 bill as 'complicated'. The World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over the law.
cite: Wikipedia 'Family Watch International'; AP and Reuters, 9 Aug 2023

n: Zambia's Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs
rank: Minister of National Guidance and Religious Affairs
d: Zambia's 1996 constitution declares it a Christian nation. President Edgar Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full ministry in September 2016 and gave its post to Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, a cleric he appointed as a nominated MP. She held it until August 2021. After the 2021 election President Hichilema dissolved the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office.
cite: Lusaka Times, 15 Sep 2016; News Diggers, 15 Sep 2021; via Wikipedia

n: Yemi Osinbajo — Redeemed Christian Church pastor as vice-president
d: The Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG) is a Nigerian Pentecostal church with branches in many countries. Osinbajo is a senior pastor of its Lagos Province 48. He was Vice President of Nigeria from 2015 to 2023 and acting president twice in 2017.
cite: BusinessDay (Lagos), 12 Apr 2022; Wikipedia biography

n: Abiy Ahmed — Pentecostal preacher as prime minister
d: Abiy converted to Pentecostal Christianity after the 1998–2000 war with Eritrea. He attends and sometimes preaches at the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church. He became prime minister in 2018 and in 2019 formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Ethiopian and international press

n: George Opare Addo — confirms he is a Freemason at minister vetting
rank: Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment
d: At his parliamentary vetting on 22 January 2025, Opare Addo was asked by Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin whether he was a Freemason and said yes, naming his lodge as 'Amity'. Afenyo-Markin had himself said in February 2024: 'I am a Freemason and a Catholic.' Opare Addo was then confirmed as minister in President Mahama's government.
cite: Graphic Online (Ghana), Jan 2025

n: Ghana — majority leader and ministers at Asantehene's Masonic jubilee
rank: Majority Leader; National Security and Transport ministers
d: In May 2024 the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, for 25 years in Freemasonry. GhanaWeb reported that National Security Minister Albert Kan-Dapaah and Transport Minister Kweku Ofori Asiamah took part as members, and that Majority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin had publicly said he is a Freemason. Former President John Kufuor has said he joined in 1967.
cite: GhanaWeb, 26 May and 1 Jun 2024

n: Macky Sall — sitting president takes Unification Church peace prize
d: The Sunhak Peace Prize is funded by the Unification Church in memory of founder Sun Myung Moon and carries a US$1 million award. In February 2020, while serving as president, Macky Sall was named a laureate alongside Lutheran bishop Munib Younan, with former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon given a separate Founders' Centenary Award.
cite: AllAfrica, 5 Feb 2020; Sunhak Peace Prize Committee

n: Hun Sen — UPF summit host and Unification Church prize-winner
d: The Universal Peace Federation (UPF) is the Unification Church's political outreach body. In November 2019 Cambodia hosted UPF's Asia-Pacific Summit at the Peace Palace, where church leader Hak Ja Han presented Prime Minister Hun Sen with a 'Leadership and Good Governance Award'. In early 2022, still in office, he received the church's Sunhak Peace Prize Founders' Award.
cite: Phnom Penh Post / Open Development Cambodia, 20 Nov 2019; Khmer Times, 31 Jan 2022

n: Donald Trump — UPF speaking fees between his two presidencies
rank: former and current President of the United States
d: Trump's revised 2023 financial disclosure listed fees from the Universal Peace Federation, the Unification Church's outreach arm, for video speeches to its summits. CNN counted $2 million for two UPF World Summits; Korean outlet Asia Economy tallied $2.5 million for three speeches: $500,000 for a September 2021 rally and $1 million each for two 2022 Seoul summits. He returned to the presidency in January 2025.
cite: US Office of Government Ethics financial disclosure, July 2023, via CNN (13 Jul 2023) and Asia Economy (25 Oct 2023)

n: Senegal's president calls on the Mouride caliph before the Magal
d: The Mourides are a Sufi brotherhood with its own holy city, Touba, which has run with wide autonomy from the state since 1928. Presidents court its caliph: Abdoulaye Wade travelled to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye visited Caliph Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 7 August 2025 ahead of the Grand Magal pilgrimage, in a pre-Magal visit that has become customary for heads of state.
cite: Seneweb, Aug 2025; Wikipedia 'Mouride' citing academic sources

n: Ahmed Toufiq — Sufi minister over Morocco's mosques since 2002
rank: Minister of Habous and Islamic Affairs
d: The Boutchichiya is Morocco's largest Sufi order. Toufiq, a historian, has said a chance meeting with the order's sheikh, al-Abbas, set him on the Sufi path; he has been the king's Minister of Islamic Affairs since November 2002 under five prime ministers. In August 2025 a leaked letter from Toufiq warned the order about 'abuses' and 'appetites' during a dispute over its leadership.
cite: Religion Unplugged, 13 Mar 2020; TelQuel, 26 Aug 2025 (headline)

n: Shah Mahmood Qureshi — shrine custodian as foreign minister
d: In Pakistan, families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines ('makhdooms' or 'pirs') draw income and votes from devotees. Qureshi's family are custodians of the Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya in Multan. He was foreign minister in 2008–11 and again under Imran Khan in 2018–22. In 2014 his brother accused him of using the saints' names for politics, which Qureshi denied.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Dawn and Pakistani press

n: Ma'ruf Amin — Nahdlatul Ulama's supreme leader becomes vice-president
d: Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) is Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, rooted in traditionalist and Sufi-influenced pesantren schools. Ma'ruf Amin was elected its supreme leader (rais 'aam) in 2015 and also chaired the Indonesian Ulema Council. President Joko Widodo picked him as running mate in August 2018; he resigned the NU post and served as vice-president from 2019 to 2024.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Indonesian press

n: Gnanasara — Bodu Bala Sena monk made head of a presidential task force
rank: chair of the Presidential Task Force on 'One Country, One Law'
d: Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist movement led by the monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, who told a 2013 rally that followers 'must become an unofficial civilian police force against Muslim extremism'. On 26 October 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed him by gazette to chair a task force on legal reform. The Bar Association said the task force would usurp the roles of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.
cite: Government gazette, 26 Oct 2021, via Daily FT; The Morning (BASL statement)

n: Supreme Court voids president's 2019 pardon of BBS leader Gnanasara
d: Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 for contempt of court in the case of disappeared journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda, and President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. He was jailed again in 2024 (four years) and January 2025 (nine months) over statements about Islam. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court ruled the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid, on petitions by the Centre for Policy Alternatives and Sandhya Eknaligoda, and in October 2026 the Court of Appeal ordered the rest of his sentence enforced.
cite: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 Sep 2026, via Daily Mirror; BBC, 10 Jan 2025

n: Ukraine bans church bodies tied to the Moscow Patriarchate
d: The Russian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate) under Patriarch Kirill backs Russia's war on Ukraine. On 20 August 2024 Ukraine's parliament adopted a law 'On the Protection of the Constitutional Order in the Field of Activities of Religious Organizations' that bans the Russian church in Ukraine and gives affiliated Ukrainian bodies nine months to cut ties. The Security Service (SBU) has raided churches of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church since 2018 and courts have sentenced individual priests.
cite: Law of Ukraine, 20 Aug 2024; via Wikipedia 'Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate)'

n: Estonia expels the Moscow Patriarchate's metropolitan
rank: Police and Border Guard Board; Riigikogu
d: The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate has about 150,000 faithful. In January 2024 Estonia refused to renew the residence permit of its head, Metropolitan Eugene (Reshetnikov), calling his support for Russia's war 'a security risk'; he left on 6 February 2024. In May 2024 the Riigikogu declared the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian military aggression, and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control.
cite: ERR News, Jan 2024 and 2025

n: Latvia's parliament orders its Orthodox Church out of Moscow's control
d: Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church. On 9 September 2022, on a bill tabled by President Egils Levits, the Saeima amended the law to make the church fully independent of any church authority outside Latvia, and required the President's chancery to be told of its bishops' appointments. No Orthodox church had recognised the new status as of mid-2026.
cite: Law on the Latvian Orthodox Church, amended 9 Sep 2022; via Wikipedia

n: UK sanctions Patriarch Kirill over support for the invasion
d: Patriarch Kirill has led the Russian Orthodox Church since 2009; Swiss federal police files classified him as a KGB agent codenamed 'Mikhailov' from 1970. In 2022 the United Kingdom, Canada and Ukraine sanctioned him, the UK citing 'multiple public statements in support of the Russian invasion of Ukraine'. An EU listing proposed in May 2022 was dropped after Hungary objected.
cite: UK sanctions notice, 2022; AFP; via Wikipedia 'Patriarch Kirill of Moscow'

n: Belgium ends Saudi control of the Great Mosque of Brussels
d: King Baudouin lent the building to Saudi Arabia in 1967 on a 99-year rent-free lease; from 1983 it was run with the Saudi-funded Muslim World League, with Gulf-trained imams. The parliamentary commission on the 2016 Brussels bombings recommended ending the concession, and on 16 March 2018 the Council of Ministers did so, citing foreign interference. In October 2017 the government had revoked the residence permit of the mosque's imam over his Salafi preaching.
cite: Belgian parliamentary commission on the 22 March 2016 attacks; Council of Ministers, 16 Mar 2018; Washington Post, 19 Mar 2018

n: Belgian State Security finds foreign agents in new Brussels mosque body
rank: Minister of Justice; State Security Service
d: After Saudi Arabia lost the Great Mosque, a new Belgian management association was set up to run it. In December 2020 Justice Minister Vincent Van Quickenborne issued a negative opinion that halted its recognition, after the State Security Service found three of its members linked to Moroccan intelligence and one employed by Turkey's Diyanet.
cite: Belgian Ministry of Justice, Dec 2020; via Wikipedia 'Great Mosque of Brussels'

n: Dutch parliamentary inquiry into Gulf and Turkish funding of mosques
d: A parliamentary inquiry chaired by CDA MP Michel Rog reported on 25 June 2020 that donors from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar funded Dutch mosques to spread a hardline Salafi Islam it called anti-democratic, and influenced the choice of imams and teaching. It listed sums such as €2.5 million to The Hague's As-Sunnah mosque (2010–17). It found that Turkey's Diyanet, whose preachers are Turkish civil servants, exerts strong political influence over Turkish-Dutch mosques.
cite: Parliamentary inquiry 'Ongewenste beïnvloeding uit onvrije landen', final report 25 Jun 2020, via DutchNews

n: Austria shuts seven mosques and reviews Turkish state imams
d: Austria's 2015 Islam law bans foreign funding of religious bodies. On 8 June 2018 Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's government said it would close one Turkish mosque and dissolve the Arab Religious Community, which ran six mosques accused of Salafi preaching. It put under review the residence permits of about 40 imams employed by ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's Diyanet, which it said had got around the funding ban. Turkey called the move 'anti-Islam' and 'racist'.
cite: Al Jazeera, 8 Jun 2018

n: Diyanet hands parliament imam reports on Gülenists in 38 countries
rank: Grand National Assembly inquiry into the coup attempt
d: The Diyanet is Turkey's state religious directorate; it employs imams as civil servants and runs over 2,000 mosques abroad. After the July 2016 coup attempt it instructed its imams abroad to gather information on followers of the Gülen movement and gave the Turkish parliament 50 intelligence reports from 38 countries. German federal prosecutors later investigated imams of its German branch, DITIB, on suspicion of informing on Gülen supporters.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 2016; Wikipedia 'Presidency of Religious Affairs'

n: Germany investigates DITIB imams for spying for Ankara
rank: Federal Prosecutor's Office; Federal Interior Ministry
d: DITIB, founded in 1984 in Cologne as a branch of Turkey's Diyanet, is one of Germany's largest Muslim organisations; its imams are Turkish civil servants. In February 2017 German federal prosecutors opened an investigation into DITIB imams suspected of passing information on Gülen supporters to Turkey. Deutsche Welle later reported, under the headline 'Court says prosecutors can't prove Turkey spies via DITIB', that the case could not be proved. The Federal Interior Ministry cut DITIB's federal funding in 2018.
cite: Politico Europe, 15 Feb 2017; DW, 5 Oct 2017 and 30 Aug 2018

n: Germany keeps Scientology under domestic intelligence watch
rank: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV)
d: Germany's domestic intelligence agency has monitored the Church of Scientology since 1997 as a group whose aims run against the constitutional order; several state agencies do the same. Scientology lost its challenge to federal surveillance in 2004, when the court relied on L. Ron Hubbard's writings that civil rights should be limited to Scientologists. The BfV estimates about 3,500 members in Germany, and monitoring continues.
cite: BfV reports; Federal court ruling, Nov 2004; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Germany'

n: Moscow court bans the Church of Scientology of Moscow
rank: Moscow City Court; Supreme Court of Russia
d: In November 2015 the Moscow City Court banned the activities of the Church of Scientology of Moscow at the request of the Justice Ministry, partly because its name is a US trademark and so, the ministry argued, not a religion. Russia's Supreme Court upheld the ban in June 2016. The European Court of Human Rights had ruled against Russia's earlier refusals to register Scientology branches in 2007 and 2009.
cite: Moscow City Court, Nov 2015; Supreme Court, Jun 2016; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Russia'

n: Belgian court acquits Scientology after 18-year case
d: Belgian prosecutors spent ten years investigating the Church of Scientology's Belgian branch and European office and in 2007 sought charges including extortion, fraud and illegal medical practice. In March 2016 the Brussels court acquitted the church and the individual defendants of all charges and rejected demands to close the branch, ruling the case inadmissible because the defendants had been 'prosecuted primarily because they were Scientologists'. Prosecutors did not appeal.
cite: Brussels court judgment, March 2016; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Belgium'

n: Paris appeal court upholds Scientology fraud conviction
d: France's government watchdog on cults (MIVILUDES) has classed Scientology as a dangerous cult since 2006. In October 2009 a Paris court convicted Scientology's Celebrity Centre and bookshop of organised fraud and fined them €600,000; it could not dissolve them because a 2009 legislative change had removed that penalty. In February 2012 the appeal court upheld the conviction, which Le Monde called a 'historic condemnation'.
cite: Paris Criminal Court, 27 Oct 2009; Le Monde, 2 Feb 2012; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in France'

n: Three members of Congress open Scientology's Washington office
rank: members of the US House of Representatives
d: In September 2012 the Church of Scientology opened a National Affairs Office near the White House. Representatives Dan Burton (R-Indiana), Sheila Jackson Lee (D-Texas) and Danny K. Davis (D-Illinois) spoke at the opening, alongside a FEMA program manager.
cite: Washingtonian, 14 Sep 2012

n: Brian Buescher — Knights of Columbus membership at judicial hearing
rank: US District Judge, District of Nebraska
d: The Knights of Columbus is a Catholic men's fraternal order founded in the United States. At Buescher's 2018 confirmation process, Senators Kamala Harris and Mazie Hirono asked about his membership, saying the order had taken 'extreme positions'; Republican senators called this a religious test barred by Article VI of the Constitution. The Senate confirmed him 51–40 on 24 July 2019 and he sits on the bench today.
cite: Senate Judiciary Committee written questions, Nov–Dec 2018; AP, 30 Dec 2018; Senate roll call, 24 Jul 2019

n: Paula White — named head of the new White House Faith Office
rank: Senior Advisor, White House Faith Office
d: The New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) is a network of self-styled apostles and prophets that seeks Christian influence over the 'seven mountains' of society, including government. Wikipedia's account of the movement lists Paula White, a televangelist and long-time spiritual adviser to Trump, among its figures. On 7 February 2025 Trump created a White House Faith Office led by White; she had been a special adviser on faith in his first term.
cite: White House announcement, Feb 2025; White House annual personnel report to Congress, 1 Jul 2025

n: Speaker Mike Johnson flies the NAR's 'Appeal to Heaven' flag
rank: Speaker of the US House of Representatives
d: Many NAR adherents use the Revolutionary-era 'Appeal to Heaven' flag to signal that Trump is chosen by God, according to scholar André Gagné. Press reports in 2024 showed the flag outside Speaker Mike Johnson's Capitol Hill office; it also flew at the vacation home of Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Johnson said in 2023 that the 'separation of church and state is a misnomer'.
cite: Press reports, 2024; André Gagné (2024); via Wikipedia 'New Apostolic Reformation'

n: Doug Mastriano — Pennsylvania senator at NAR events
rank: Pennsylvania state senator and 2022 governor nominee
d: Mastriano has sat in the Pennsylvania Senate since 2019 and was the Republican nominee for governor in 2022. Salon and Media Matters reported that he attended NAR events and campaigned with Julie Green, an NAR 'prophet' who gave the opening prayer at one of his events. He worships at a Mennonite church.
cite: Salon, Jul 2022; Media Matters, Aug 2022

n: William Barr — Opus Dei centre board member to attorney general
rank: Attorney General of the United States
d: The Catholic Information Center in Washington is run by Opus Dei priests and is a meeting place for politically connected Catholics. Barr sat on its board from 2014 to 2017 and became Trump's attorney general in February 2019. Opus Dei has said Barr is not a member.
cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Washington Post and America magazine

n: Guillermo Lasso — Opus Dei supernumerary as president of Ecuador
d: Supernumeraries are married lay members of Opus Dei. Lasso, a banker, has been reported as a supernumerary since at least 2009 (El Universo). He was President of Ecuador from May 2021 to November 2023.
cite: El Universo, 2009; Wikipedia 'Guillermo Lasso' and 'List of members of Opus Dei'

n: Przemysław Wipler — Opus Dei supernumerary in Poland's Sejm
d: Gazeta Wyborcza reported Wipler as an Opus Dei supernumerary as of 2023. He was elected to the Sejm for the Confederation in October 2023 and in January 2024 became vice-chair of the parliamentary inquiry into the previous government's use of Pegasus spyware.
cite: Gazeta Wyborcza, 2023; Sejm records; via Wikipedia

n: Luis Silva — Opus Dei numerary as Chile's under-secretary of justice
d: Silva, a law professor, is an Opus Dei numerary, as La Tercera and El País reported when he topped the 2023 vote for Chile's Constitutional Council for the Republican Party. He took office as Undersecretary of Justice under President José Antonio Kast on 11 March 2026.
cite: La Tercera, 8 May 2023; El País Chile, 12 May 2023; Government of Chile appointment, Mar 2026

n: José Antonio Kast — Schoenstatt Movement member as president
d: The Schoenstatt Movement is a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914, present in over 110 countries, with 25 shrines in Chile. Kast is a practising Catholic and a member of the movement, as El Mercurio reported in a 2011 profile of his family. He took office as President of Chile in March 2026.
cite: El Mercurio, 31 Jul 2011; via Wikipedia biography

n: Eddie Villanueva — Jesus Is Lord Church founder as deputy speaker
rank: Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives
d: The Jesus Is Lord Church Worldwide is a Philippine evangelical church; Villanueva is its founder and spiritual director and also founded the Philippines for Jesus Movement. After presidential runs in 2004 and 2010, he entered the House in 2019 for the CIBAC party-list and was a Deputy Speaker from July 2019 to June 2022. His son Joel Villanueva is a senator.
cite: House of Representatives records; Wikipedia biography

n: Fabricio Alvarado — Christian singer's party in Costa Rica's assembly
rank: Legislative Assembly deputy and presidential runoff candidate
d: Alvarado is an evangelical Christian singer and former journalist. As the only deputy of the National Restoration Party he reached the 2018 presidential runoff on opposition to an Inter-American Court ruling on same-sex marriage, losing to Carlos Alvarado. He founded the New Republic Party in 2019 and sat in the Legislative Assembly again from 2022 to 2026.
cite: CRHoy; Costa Rican electoral tribunal results; via Wikipedia biography

n: Senator books Bellas Artes for La Luz del Mundo leader's homage
rank: Senator; National Institute of Fine Arts (INBAL)
d: La Luz del Mundo is a Guadalajara-based church with members in many countries. Senator Rogelio Zamora Guzmán (PVEM, allied with Morena) wrote to INBAL in January 2019 asking for the Palacio de Bellas Artes; on 15 May 2019 it hosted a homage for leader Naasón Joaquín García's 50th birthday. INBAL said it had been told it was an opera gala. García was arrested in Los Angeles in June 2019 and in June 2022 pleaded guilty to child sexual abuse, receiving 16 years and 8 months.
cite: SDP Noticias; Los Angeles Times, 3 Jun 2022; New York Times, 9 Jun 2022

n: Cuba's ex-Grand Master admits he was a state-security officer
rank: Department of State Security (Ministry of the Interior)
d: José Manuel Collera Vento became Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Cuba in 2000 after government pressure. In 2011, after WikiLeaks cables exposed him, he admitted on the state TV series 'Las Razones de Cuba' that he had worked for state security as 'Agente Gerardo' and had been placed as Grand Master so the government could monitor Freemasons. The Pinar del Río provincial assembly gave him its highest award in April 2011.
cite: Las Razones de Cuba (Cuban state TV), 2011; CNN; via Wikipedia 'Freemasonry in Cuba'

n: Cuban Justice Ministry steps into the Grand Lodge leadership crisis
d: In January 2024 about $19,000 kept in the Grand Master's office safe for a Masonic retirement home went missing, and Grand Master Mario Urquía Carreño was expelled amid the dispute. Cuba's Ministry of Justice, which registers associations, then intervened and declined to recognise the lodge's newly elected leadership, 14ymedio reported. A former grand official who fled in 2023 said a state-security officer had told him agents had watched Cuban lodges for over 40 years.
cite: 14ymedio, 2024; via Wikipedia 'Freemasonry in Cuba'

n: Pope rewrites the Order of Malta's constitution and council
rank: Holy See over the Sovereign Council of the Order of Malta
d: The Sovereign Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that is also a sovereign entity with diplomatic relations with 115 states and UN observer status. In January 2017 Pope Francis forced Grand Master Matthew Festing to resign after a dispute over Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager. On 3 September 2022 Francis promulgated a new constitution for the order and appointed its Sovereign Council himself; the order's chapter re-elected his appointees in January 2023.
cite: Holy See decree, 3 Sep 2022; Wikipedia 'Sovereign Military Order of Malta'

n: Juan Orlando Hernández — President 2014–2022
d: Convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to import cocaine and related weapons counts, and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. His brother, a former congressman, was convicted in the same district in 2018. He was granted a full and unconditional US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and released the same day; Honduras then asked Interpol to execute a 2023 domestic arrest order written to take effect if US authorities freed him. The conviction stands and the sentence goes unserved.
cite: US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y., verdict March 2024, sentence June 2024; presidential pardon 1 December 2025; Honduran Ministerio Publico arrest order, December 2025
undone: Pardoned by the US president in December 2025; released the same day.

n: Genaro Garcia Luna — Secretary of Public Security 2006–2012
d: The cabinet minister who ran Mexico’s federal police during the militarised phase of the drug war was convicted in the Eastern District of New York on all five counts, including continuing criminal enterprise, of taking Sinaloa Cartel payments in exchange for protection from arrest, safe passage for shipments and warnings of coming operations. He was sentenced in 2024. In May 2025 a US court ordered him and his wife to pay Mexico more than .4 billion in a civil suit over public contracts, which is the largest financial judgment attached to any official on this map.
cite: US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., verdict February 2023, sentence 2024; US civil judgment for the Government of Mexico, May 2025

n: Manuel Noriega — head of state 1983–1989
d: Convicted in Miami federal court of drug trafficking, racketeering and money laundering after the US invasion removed him. The earliest case in which a sitting head of state's control of the security apparatus was prosecuted as a trafficking enterprise.
cite: US v. Noriega, S.D. Fla., 1992

n: Desi Bouterse — head of state, later President
d: Convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced to eleven years; with no extradition treaty the sentence was never executed and he was subsequently elected president twice. A separate 16-year Surinamese prosecution over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents produced a 20-year sentence upheld finally in December 2023. He did not surrender, vanished in January 2024, and died in hiding in December 2024 having served no time on either conviction.
cite: Court of The Hague, cocaine conviction in absentia July 1999; Court of Justice of Suriname, December Murders verdict upheld 20 December 2023; death reported December 2024

n: Jose Americo Bubo Na Tchuto — Navy chief of staff
d: The head of the navy was taken in a DEA sting in international waters and pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine into the United States. The country's air force chief was indicted in the same operation.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y., plea 2014

n: Parapolitica — the Congress investigations
d: Roughly 30% of the Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the AUC paramilitaries, who were themselves among the country's largest cocaine traffickers. By April 2012, 139 members of Congress were under investigation; five governors and 32 legislators had been convicted. A later Inspector General review counted more than 500 elected officials investigated over a decade.
cite: Supreme Court of Justice proceedings from 2006; Human Rights Watch; Procuraduria General

n: Vladimiro Montesinos — intelligence chief
d: Head of the national intelligence service under Fujimori and, in practice, of the military, the courts and much of the press. He was convicted on a long series of counts including drug trafficking, and separately sentenced to twenty years for arranging an airdrop of ten thousand assault rifles to Colombian guerrillas. He was accused of sixty-three offences in all and pleaded guilty in 2024 to homicide and forced disappearance in the 1992 killing of six farmers. He videotaped himself paying bribes, which is how much of the record exists: the agency nominally responsible for counter-narcotics kept its own evidence.
cite: Peruvian Supreme Court convictions from 2006; arms-trafficking verdict September 2006; guilty plea, January 2024

n: Rene Sanabria — head of the anti-drug police
d: The former commander of the FELCN, the national anti-narcotics force, and since 2009 head of an elite drug intelligence unit inside the Interior Ministry, was taken in a DEA sting: his group agreed to protect Miami-bound cocaine loads for a 50,000 payment, and one container shipment was seized on arrival. He pleaded guilty in Miami and was sentenced in September 2011 to 14 years, his co-defendant to nine.
cite: US v. Sanabria-Oropeza and Foronda-Azero, S.D. Fla., pleas June 2011, sentences 23 September 2011

n: Edgar Veytia — Attorney General of Nayarit
d: The chief prosecutor of a Mexican state pleaded guilty in Brooklyn to a conspiracy to import heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, and was sentenced in September 2019 to 20 years with  million in forfeiture. Prosecutors established that between 2013 and 2017 he used the office for the H-2 cartel: directing officers to wiretap and arrest rival traffickers, releasing the cartel’s members from custody, and assisting acts of violence. He had campaigned on the claim that there was no room for organised crime in Nayarit. His governor, Roberto Sandoval, was designated by Treasury two months earlier.
cite: US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., guilty plea 2019, sentence 26 September 2019 before Judge Carol Bagley Amon

n: Tomas Yarrington — Governor of Tamaulipas
d: Governor of Tamaulipas from 1999 to 2005 and a presidential candidate, he fled Mexico in 2012, was arrested in Italy in 2017 and extradited the following year. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and was sentenced in March 2023 to nine years, having admitted taking more than .5 million in bribes; prosecutors put the laundered total at between .5 and .5 million over fourteen years. The charges that described the trade itself — conspiracy to import cocaine and marijuana, bank fraud — were dismissed under the plea. He was released in November 2024 after a sentence adjustment for time served and returned to Mexico in April 2025 to face a second laundering case.
cite: US v. Yarrington Ruvalcaba, S.D. Tex., plea 25 March 2021, sentence 15 March 2023; Bureau of Prisons release records, 2024; Fiscalia General de la Republica proceedings, 2025

n: Cartel de los Soles indictment
rank: head of state and general staff
d: The US Department of Justice indicted Nicolas Maduro and more than a dozen serving and former officials, including senior military commanders, on narco-terrorism and cocaine importation charges in 2020. Treasury designated the group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in July 2025 and the State Department as a Foreign Terrorist Organization from 24 November 2025, saying the regime had corrupted parts of the military, intelligence apparatus, legislature and judiciary to serve it. That designation underpinned a maritime campaign in the Caribbean and Pacific and Maduro was taken into custody on 3 January 2026. Analysts and former officials dispute that it is a formally organised cartel or that he leads one, while agreeing there is government involvement in the trade; the charges have not been tried.
cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; OFAC SDGT designation July 2025; State Department FTO designation effective 24 November 2025; capture reported 3 January 2026

n: Metastasis — judges, prosecutors and police
d: Decryption of a trafficker’s phone produced charges against judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials over case-fixing and protection, the broadest judicial-capture case in the country’s history. After 28 days of hearings the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants in November 2024 to between three and ten years, with public service treated as an aggravating factor. The former president of the Judiciary Council drew nine years and four months for delaying a habeas corpus in favour of a trafficker’s brother for money; another judge was convicted over a release order priced at 00,000. The court sent its ruling back to prosecutors to investigate judges, prosecutors, journalists and lawyers named at trial but never charged. Two fugitives, a former legislator and a businessman, are the subject of extradition requests to Venezuela and the United States.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Metastasis, from December 2023; Corte Nacional de Justicia verdicts, 25 November 2024; extradition requests, 2026

n: Saimir Tahiri — Interior Minister
d: The former interior minister was prosecuted over links to a cannabis-trafficking network and convicted of abuse of office; the trafficking counts did not result in conviction. The case is the clearest test of ministerial-level capture inside an EU candidate state.
cite: Tirana courts, conviction 2019, upheld on appeal

n: Ousmane Conte — son of the head of state
d: Arrested in February 2009 by the junta that took power after the death of his father, the head of state, and charged with trafficking. He confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade; it was not clear whether the confession was coerced. Treasury designated him a kingpin in 2010 while he was held in a Conakry prison and standing trial. No verdict from a competent court followed, which is the pattern across the West African corridor: the admission exists, the judgment does not.
cite: Guinean state television broadcast, February 2009; OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2010

n: 'Ndrangheta and local administration — Calabria
d: The Rinascita-Scott proceedings convicted officials, lawyers and elected representatives alongside clan members. The organisation is assessed by European law enforcement as controlling a large share of cocaine entering Europe, and dozens of Calabrian municipal councils have been dissolved for mafia infiltration under Italian law.
cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia / Catanzaro, Rinascita-Scott verdicts from 2021

n: Port of Antwerp — customs, police and port workers
d: Successive prosecutions have convicted port workers, police officers and customs staff for extracting containers and passing information, in the port through which the largest cocaine volumes in Europe move. In 2022 the Belgian justice minister was placed under protection after a kidnap plot.
cite: Antwerp criminal court proceedings, multiple, 2018–2024

n: Marengo — police and judicial leaks
d: During the Marengo trial a lawyer and a police employee were among those prosecuted for passing protected information to a trafficking network; a witness's lawyer and brother were murdered during the proceedings.
cite: Amsterdam District Court, Marengo proceedings, 2018–2024

n: Captagon production and the state
d: The United States enacted the Captagon Act directing an interagency strategy against production assessed as linked to the Syrian government and associated networks; the UK and EU imposed sanctions on named figures. The assessments are governmental rather than judicial.
cite: Captagon Act (US, 2022); UK and EU sanctions designations, 2023

n: Kamchybek Kolbayev — designated kingpin with state protection
d: Designated under the US Kingpin Act, repeatedly released or lightly sentenced by domestic courts, and killed in a security operation in 2023. The record of releases is the documentary trace of protection.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2011; Kyrgyz court records

n: Provincial power and the opium economy
d: Successive US government and UN assessments described provincial officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium production. Very little of it reached a courtroom, which is itself the finding.
cite: UNODC Afghanistan Opium Surveys; US SIGAR reporting

n: Border militias inside the state structure — Shan State
d: Armed groups formally incorporated into the state as border guard forces operate in the areas producing the largest volumes of methamphetamine assessed anywhere. Myanmar scores 10 out of 10 on the synthetic drug indicator and 9 on state-embedded actors.
cite: UNODC Synthetic Drugs in East and Southeast Asia; GI-TOC country profile

n: Municipal police forces disbanded for cartel control
d: Whole municipal forces in Michoacan, Guerrero, Tamaulipas and elsewhere have been disarmed, disbanded or federalised after being assessed as working for trafficking groups. The remedy is administrative, so almost none of it produces a conviction record.
cite: Mexican federal and state government disbandment orders, various

n: Juan Antonio 'Tony' Hernandez — member of Congress
d: The president's brother was convicted in Manhattan of importing cocaine, weapons offences and false statements, and sentenced to life plus 30 years. Trial evidence included cocaine packages stamped TH and testimony that the proceeds funded the National Party's campaigns.
cite: US v. Juan Antonio Hernandez Alvarado, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2019, sentence March 2021

n: Juan Carlos 'El Tigre' Bonilla — national police chief 2012–2013
d: Extradited in 2022, he pleaded guilty in February 2024 to a cocaine trafficking conspiracy and was sentenced to 19 years. Prosecutors said he took payments to provide armed protection for loads crossing the country; he maintains through his family that the plea was tactical.
cite: US v. Bonilla Valladares, S.D.N.Y., plea February 2024, sentence August 2024

n: Fabio Lobo — son of President Porfirio Lobo
d: Arrested in Haiti in a DEA sting, he pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine and was sentenced to 24 years. He had arranged police escorts for shipments he believed belonged to the Cachiros.
cite: US v. Fabio Porfirio Lobo, S.D.N.Y., plea 2016, sentence September 2017

n: Rosenthal family and Grupo Continental
d: A former vice-president, his son — a congressman and later presidential candidate — and a nephew were designated by OFAC as launderers for the Cachiros; the family's bank was liquidated by Honduran regulators within weeks. Yani Rosenthal pleaded guilty in New York in 2017 and served three years.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, October 2015; US v. Yankel Rosenthal, S.D.N.Y., plea 2017

n: Mario Villanueva Madrid — Governor of Quintana Roo 1993–1999
d: Convicted in Mexico and then extradited, he pleaded guilty in Manhattan to laundering proceeds of the Juarez Cartel, which had used the state's coast and airstrips with his protection. He served US and Mexican sentences consecutively across two decades.
cite: US v. Villanueva Madrid, S.D.N.Y., plea 2010, sentence 2011

n: Ivan Reyes Arzate — commander, Federal Police Sensitive Investigative Unit
d: The officer who ran the unit vetted by US agencies for shared intelligence took a $290,000 payment in 2016 to tell the El Seguimiento 39 cartel what that joint investigation knew. He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn and was sentenced to ten years.
cite: US v. Reyes Arzate, E.D.N.Y., plea October 2021, sentence February 2022

n: Salvador Cienfuegos — Secretary of National Defence 2012–2018
d: Arrested in Los Angeles in October 2020 on trafficking and laundering charges, he was released a month later when the Department of Justice dismissed the case at the request of the State Department after Mexico threatened its security cooperation. Mexico's own inquiry closed in 2021 without charges.
cite: US v. Cienfuegos Zepeda, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2019, dismissal November 2020; FGR statement January 2021
undone: Charges dismissed by the Department of Justice at the State Department’s request after Mexico threatened security cooperation.

n: Adan Castillo — director of the anti-narcotics police (SAIA)
d: The head of Guatemala's lead anti-drug agency and his deputy operations chief were arrested during a US-funded training visit to Virginia and pleaded guilty in Washington to conspiring to distribute cocaine bound for the United States.
cite: US v. Castillo Aguilar and Aguilar Garcia, D.D.C., pleas September 2006

n: Roxana Baldetti and Mauricio Lopez Bonilla — Vice-President and Interior Minister
d: Both were indicted in Washington in 2016 on a single count of conspiring to distribute cocaine knowing it would be imported to the United States, over conduct alleged between 2010 and 2015. She denies it. The drug charge has never been tried: a Guatemalan court approved extradition only after her domestic cases are resolved, and those have taken her instead through separate corruption convictions — 15 and a half years in 2018 over a lake-cleaning contract whose chemical proved to be water, salt and chlorine, and 16 years in 2022 for customs fraud. She has been in Guatemalan custody throughout on charges other than the one on this map.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment 2016; Guatemalan convictions October 2018 and 2022; extradition approved subject to prior resolution of domestic cases

n: Romeo Ramos Cruz — mayor of Santa Lucia, Escuintla
d: Extradited in August 2025, the mayor of Santa Lucia in Escuintla pleaded guilty to conspiring to import cocaine.
