From 2022 to 2024 he used the office to coordinate logistics for a trafficking organisation: in one instance agreeing to disguise a shipment from Venezuela as a delivery of cement, and preparing a letter on official municipal letterhead to help it evade inspection. He faces a maximum of life.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, extradition August 2025, guilty plea July 2026

n: Freddy Salazar Flores — Central American Parliament deputy
d: A sitting PARLACEN representative and his father-in-law, named by prosecutors as leaders of the Huistas organisation on the Mexican border, appeared in a Washington court in May 2025 on a 2017 indictment charging cocaine importation. Neither has been tried.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, indictment 2017, initial appearances May 2025

n: Prison and social-fabric officials — the gang negotiations
d: The US Treasury designated the director of prisons and the head of the Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit for negotiating with MS-13 and Barrio 18 leaders — privileges and money inside the prisons in exchange for lower homicide figures and electoral support. The government denies the finding, and no case has been tried.
cite: OFAC designations, December 2021; El Faro reporting from 2020

n: General Mauricio Santoyo — presidential security chief
d: The national police general who ran security for President Uribe pleaded guilty in Virginia to providing material support to the AUC, then among Colombia's largest cocaine exporters, and was sentenced to 13 years.
cite: US v. Santoyo Velasco, E.D. Va., plea August 2012

n: Hugo Carvajal — director of military intelligence
d: Extradited from Spain in 2023, he pleaded guilty in June 2025 to cocaine importation, narco-terrorism for the benefit of the FARC and weapons counts. Prosecutors describe him as a leader of the Cartel de los Soles, the network they say runs through the officer corps itself.
cite: US v. Carvajal Barrios, S.D.N.Y., plea June 2025

n: Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas — the first lady's nephews
d: Two nephews of Cilia Flores were arrested in Haiti after offering 800 kilograms of cocaine to DEA informants, convicted in Manhattan and sentenced to 18 years. Both were released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in 2022.
cite: US v. Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas, S.D.N.Y., verdict November 2016; prisoner exchange October 2022
undone: Both released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in October 2022, six years into 18-year sentences.

n: Maximiliano Davila — director of the anti-narcotics force (FELCN)
d: The head of the FELCN until 2019 was convicted at trial in Manhattan in October 2025 and sentenced to 25 years. Prosecutors showed he steered investigations away from allied traffickers and assigned armed FELCN officers under his command to guard cocaine loads.
cite: US v. Davila Perez, S.D.N.Y., verdict October 2025, sentence March 2026

n: A Ultranza Py — the 2022 network case
d: A cocaine and laundering investigation opened in February 2022 produced charges against police officers, prosecutors and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, and the seizure of hundreds of properties. The central figure fled before arrest and the proceedings continue.
cite: Ministerio Publico del Paraguay, Operativo A Ultranza Py, from February 2022

n: Dino Bouterse — head of the counter-terrorism unit, son of the President
rank: security unit chief and presidential family
d: While running Suriname's counter-terrorism unit he was lured to Panama, arrested, and pleaded guilty in New York to cocaine importation, weapons offences and offering Hezbollah a base in the country. He was sentenced to 16 years.
cite: US v. Dino Bouterse, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2014, sentence March 2015

n: Guy Philippe — senator-elect and former police commander
d: Seized in Port-au-Prince days after winning a Senate seat, he pleaded guilty in Miami to conspiring to launder drug proceeds and was sentenced to nine years. He was deported to Haiti in 2023 and re-entered politics on arrival.
cite: US v. Guy Philippe, S.D. Fla., plea April 2017; deportation November 2023

n: Tivoli Gardens and the Coke extradition
rank: head of government and security forces
d: The government resisted a US extradition request for Christopher Coke for nine months, retaining a Washington law firm to lobby against it; the incursion that followed killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. The commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in its conduct, and the prime minister had already resigned over the affair.
cite: US v. Christopher Coke, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2011; West Kingston Commission of Enquiry report, 2016

n: General Arnaldo Ochoa and the Interior Ministry — Case No. 1 of 1989
rank: army general and interior ministry officers
d: A decorated general and a Ministry of the Interior colonel who ran the state's hard-currency operations were court-martialled for trafficking cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace, and executed by firing squad in July 1989. The interior minister was dismissed and jailed in the same purge.
cite: Cuban special military tribunal, Causa No. 1, June–July 1989

n: Air force sergeant on the presidential delegation flight
d: A sergeant travelling with the presidential delegation to the G20 was caught in Seville with 39 kilograms of cocaine in his luggage aboard an air force aircraft. He was convicted by a Brazilian military court and sentenced to over ten years.
cite: Superior Tribunal Militar, conviction 2019; Spanish Guardia Civil seizure, June 2019

n: Hugo Tognoli — chief of the Santa Fe provincial police
d: The officer who had headed the province's drug unit before taking command of its police was convicted of protecting a trafficking network around Rosario and sentenced to six years. The city's homicide rate has since run several times the national figure.
cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Rosario, conviction 2016

n: Operation Guard Shack — Puerto Rico police
d: Eighty-nine law enforcement officers and 44 others were charged after 125 undercover transactions in which officers guarded cocaine deals for $500 to $4,500 apiece. Around 750 FBI personnel were flown in for the arrests; the Bureau called it the largest police corruption case in its history.
cite: US v. Rivera Guzman et al. and 25 related indictments, D.P.R., October 2010

n: Baltimore Gun Trace Task Force
d: An elite plainclothes squad was convicted of racketeering after robbing residents and dealers, reselling seized narcotics through a bail bondsman, and claiming overtime for hours not worked. Prosecutors and the courts have since reviewed hundreds of cases the unit built.
cite: US v. Gondo et al. and US v. Hersl and Taylor, D. Md., pleas and verdicts 2017–2018
who: Baltimore drug dealers and resale network

n: Jose Irizarry — DEA special agent
d: An agent assigned to money-laundering operations in Colombia diverted laundered funds to himself and his associates, and was sentenced to 12 years. He had used the agency's own undercover accounts, which is why the losses took years to surface.
cite: US v. Irizarry, M.D. Fla., plea 2020, sentence November 2021

n: Ronald Watts — Chicago police sergeant
d: A sergeant and his tactical team ran a protection racket in a public housing development, taxing dealers and framing those who refused. He pleaded guilty to a federal theft charge; courts have since vacated more than 200 convictions built on his team's word.
cite: US v. Watts, N.D. Ill., plea 2013; Cook County exoneration orders from 2017

n: Cameron Ortis — RCMP intelligence director
d: The civilian head of the RCMP's National Intelligence Coordination Centre was convicted under the Security of Information Act of offering operational material to targets, among them the head of the encrypted-phone firm Phantom Secure. He was sentenced to 14 years.
cite: R v. Ortis, Ontario Superior Court, verdict November 2023, sentence February 2024

n: The Djindjic assassination — the JSO and the Zemun clan
d: The prime minister was shot in 2003 by a serving commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had merged with a Zemun criminal group holding a share of the Balkan heroin trade. Twelve were convicted in 2007; the unit was disbanded.
cite: Special Court for Organised Crime, Belgrade, verdicts May 2007

n: Chief special prosecutor, police command and the Kavac clan
d: Sky ECC transcripts passed to Podgorica by Europol produced charges against the former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer, over protection of the Kavac clan's cocaine trade. Separate indictments name a former president of the Supreme Court, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva.
cite: Special State Prosecutor's Office of Montenegro, indictments 2023–2024

n: The Susurluk crash
d: A car crash near Susurluk killed a deputy police chief, a wanted trafficker and hitman carrying a diplomatic passport, and left a member of parliament injured. The parliamentary commission that followed documented the working relationship between the security apparatus and heroin trafficking, and produced almost no convictions.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk commission report, 1997

n: Moscow drug squad officers — the Golunov case
d: Five officers of a Moscow district drug unit were convicted of planting narcotics on a journalist and sentenced to between five and twelve years. The case is the rare Russian instance where the fabrication of a drug charge by serving officers reached a verdict.
cite: Moscow City Court, verdict 2022

n: The OCRTIS 'coups d'achat' file
d: The former head of the national anti-drug office was placed under formal investigation over cannabis shipments run through an informer, in a case turning on how far a police service may let a trade operate to reach the people behind it. He denies wrongdoing.
cite: French judicial investigation opened 2019, Paris; Cour de cassation rulings on related seizures

n: Operation Venetic — officers among those convicted
d: The EncroChat material produced thousands of UK prosecutions, among them serving police and prison officers who had sold information or moved contraband. The corruption was found by reading the traffickers' messages rather than by internal detection.
cite: National Crime Agency Operation Venetic reporting, from 2020

n: Cai Dongjia — party secretary of Boshe village, Lufeng
d: Three thousand police raided the village in December 2013 and seized three tonnes of methamphetamine; officials put a fifth of its households in the trade and said Boshe had supplied a third of China's meth. The party secretary who had shielded the labs and tipped off suspects was sentenced to death in 2016 and executed in 2019; a Lufeng drug squad captain was detained in the same investigation.
cite: Guangdong Higher People's Court, sentence 2016; Xinhua, execution January 2019

n: The Pong Su — a state-linked vessel
d: A North Korean freighter delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria in 2003 and was boarded by Australian special forces. The captain and senior crew were acquitted of importation in 2006 — the jury was not persuaded they knew the cargo — and the ship was later sunk as a bombing target. The state link was never established in court.
cite: R v. Song and others, Supreme Court of Victoria, acquittals March 2006

n: Teddy Minahasa — police inspector general
d: A two-star general days from taking command of the Jakarta police was convicted of ordering seized methamphetamine to be replaced with alum and sold on. Prosecutors sought death; the court imposed life imprisonment, later reduced on appeal.
cite: West Jakarta District Court, verdict May 2023

n: The 'ninja cops' and recycled seizures
d: A Senate inquiry examined officers who reported partial seizures and resold the rest, a practice known locally as ninja cops. The chief of the national police resigned in October 2019 over his handling of a 2013 case in Pampanga; the administrative and criminal proceedings that followed produced no senior conviction.
cite: Philippine Senate Committee on Public Order hearings, 2019; PNP internal affairs records

n: Narcotics Control Bureau — the Mumbai zonal office
d: The CBI registered a case in 2023 against the former zonal director of the Narcotics Control Bureau in Mumbai and three colleagues, alleging a demand for payment to keep a name out of a high-profile cruise-ship seizure file. He denies the allegation and the case has not been tried.
cite: Central Bureau of Investigation FIR, May 2023; Bombay High Court proceedings

n: Abdur Rahman Bodi — member of parliament for Cox's Bazar
d: The MP for the district through which almost all yaba enters Bangladesh appeared on the government's own list of traffickers. He was convicted in 2018 of concealing wealth and jailed for three years; the trafficking allegations themselves were never brought to trial, and 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered in a staged ceremony in 2019.
cite: Dhaka Special Judge's Court, Anti-Corruption Commission case, conviction February 2018

n: Ahmed Wali Karzai — Kandahar provincial council
rank: provincial council chairman and presidential family
d: The president's half-brother, who chaired the Kandahar provincial council and was reported to be on the CIA payroll, was described by US officials as a participant in the opium trade. He denied it, was never charged in any court, and was shot dead by his own security chief in 2011.
cite: US State Department and military reporting, 2009–2010; SIGAR and UNODC assessments

n: Raiymbek Matraimov — deputy chief of customs
d: Designated by the US Treasury under the Magnitsky Act for a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Journalists who documented the network were prosecuted or forced out; he settled a domestic corruption case by repayment and served no prison term at the time.
cite: OFAC Global Magnitsky designation, December 2020; OCCRP and Kloop investigations 2019–2020

n: Captagon on a private jet — the Beirut airport arrest
d: A member of the Saudi royal family and four others were detained at Beirut airport in October 2015 while loading two tonnes of captagon onto a private jet. Lebanese prosecutors charged them; no verdict in the case has been made public.
cite: Lebanese Internal Security Forces statement and public prosecution filing, October 2015

n: The Akasha file — judges, prosecutors and police
d: Two brothers running a Mombasa heroin organisation pleaded guilty in New York, and their obstruction count was an admission that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police officers over two years to block their extradition. None of the officials who took the money has been named or charged in Kenya.
cite: US v. Baktash Akasha Abdalla et al., S.D.N.Y., pleas October 2018, sentences 2019

n: Abba Kyari — deputy commissioner of police
d: The head of the police Intelligence Response Team was charged by the drug agency with substituting seized cocaine and offering an officer 1,400 to stop it being tested. In March 2026 a judge acquitted him and two brothers on a separate 23-count asset-declaration charge, describing that prosecution as persecution. The cocaine trial continues before a different judge alongside four suspended officers of his unit; two traffickers originally charged with them pleaded guilty and were jailed. He has been in detention since 2022.
cite: NDLEA charges, Federal High Court Abuja, from February 2022; acquittal on asset-declaration counts, March 2026; substantive drug trial continuing before Justice Nwite

n: Ibraima Papa Camara — air force chief of staff
d: Indicted in New York alongside the navy chief for conspiring to store and move cocaine through the country, and named earlier by the US Treasury as a trafficker. He remained in Bissau and was never surrendered.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto and Camara, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013; OFAC Kingpin designation 2010

n: The MV Benjamin cocaine and the Boakye tapes
d: Seventy-seven parcels of cocaine landed from a vessel and disappeared; a recording then surfaced of a senior police officer meeting suspects at his home. The committee of enquiry led by a Supreme Court judge found the police account unsatisfactory, and the officer returned to duty.
cite: Georgina Wood Committee report, Government of Ghana, 2006

n: Air Cocaine — the Tarkint airstrip
d: A Boeing 727 that had flown from Venezuela was unloaded at a desert strip and then burned. UN and national investigations pointed to protection by local officials and armed groups; the arrests made in Bamako produced no senior conviction, and the aircraft's owners were never established.
cite: UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010; Malian judicial proceedings

n: Christiaan Prinsloo — police colonel, firearms to the Cape gangs
d: A colonel sold roughly two thousand firearms from police stores to Cape Flats gangs, and was sentenced to 18 years. Ballistics have since linked the guns to more than a thousand shootings, many of them in the drug turf conflicts of the Flats.
cite: Bellville Regional Court, plea and sentence 2016; SAPS ballistics evidence

n: Hernan Bermudez Requena — Secretary of Security of Tabasco
d: The state's top police official from 2018 to 2024 is accused of running La Barredora, a group tied to the CJNG, from the office itself. He fled Mexico in early 2025, was arrested in Paraguay in September and returned within days; he is held at the Altiplano federal prison on criminal association, extortion and kidnapping charges.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado de Tabasco warrant, February 2025; Paraguayan SENAD arrest and expulsion, September 2025

n: Piedras Negras prison, Coahuila
d: A state prison was used by Los Zetas as a base, workshop and disposal site, with the administration handing over control of parts of the facility. Testimony in Texas trials and a state investigation established the arrangement; the prosecutions that followed reached staff rather than the officials who authorised it.
cite: Coahuila state attorney general investigation, 2016–2017; testimony in US v. Trevino Morales, W.D. Tex.

n: Jose Armando Ubico Aguilar — member of Congress 2016–2024
d: Indicted in Texas in 2021 while sitting in Congress, he pleaded guilty in May 2024 to an international trafficking conspiracy, admitting he passed drug-related information and cash to another Guatemalan official on a trafficker's behalf.
cite: US v. Ubico Aguilar, E.D. Tex., indictment March 2021, plea May 2024

n: Cliver Alcala Cordones — retired army major general
d: Charged in the same 2020 indictment as Maduro, he surrendered to the DEA in Colombia, pleaded guilty to providing material support including firearms to the FARC, and was sentenced to 260 months in April 2024. He is the first of that indictment's defendants to be sentenced.
cite: US v. Alcala Cordones, S.D.N.Y., plea 2023, sentence April 2024

n: Campo de Gibraltar police — the Algeciras cases
d: A municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced in April 2024 to more than seven years each for guarding a 367-kilogram cocaine load. A separate 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers at the port of Algeciras along with an officer stationed in Ceuta, a customs official and a former police official, over 6.2 tonnes moved through the strait.
cite: Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz, sentence April 2024; Policia Nacional operation, Algeciras, 2022

n: Antwerp police arrests and the Brussels mega-trial
d: Twenty-two people including three serving police officers were arrested in January 2024 over cocaine moving through Antwerp. In October 2024 a Brussels court sentenced dozens in the country's largest trafficking trial, built almost entirely on decrypted Sky ECC and EncroChat traffic; 116 tonnes of cocaine were seized at the port in 2023 alone.
cite: Belgian federal police operation, January 2024; Brussels correctional court verdicts, October 2024

n: Inez Weski — defence counsel in the Marengo case
d: The lawyer for Ridouan Taghi was arrested in April 2023 on suspicion of relaying messages between her client in a maximum-security prison and his organisation, using the privileged channel between counsel and detainee. She had sold her law office to her son and formally retired ten days before the arrest. The Rotterdam District Court convicted her in May 2026 of participating in the organisation, and set the sentence equal to the 42 days she had already spent in pre-trial detention, so she served no further time. Taghi himself was sentenced to life in February 2024.
cite: Rechtbank Rotterdam, conviction May 2026; Openbaar Ministerie arrest April 2023; Taghi life sentence, February 2024

n: Hanoi and Phu Tho narcotics officers
d: Two former officers of a Hanoi district drug investigation team were indicted in 2024 for shielding a Laos–Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms; a senior officer in Viet Tri was sentenced to life in 2025 for financing a 12,000-tablet purchase he intended to convert into a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers at these weights, which is the measure of what the officers were protecting.
cite: Supreme People's Procuracy indictments, 2024; Hanoi People's Court verdict, 2025

n: Tareck El Aissami — Executive Vice-President
d: Designated under the Kingpin Act weeks after his appointment as vice-president, for facilitating shipments out of Venezuela and protecting traffickers operating inside it. Treasury designated his frontman and a network of petroleum, engineering and holding companies at the same time. The finding is executive, not judicial, and has never been tested at trial.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, February 2017

n: Isidro Avelar Gutierrez — federal magistrate judge
d: A sitting federal magistrate was designated under the Kingpin Act for taking payments from the CJNG and Los Cuinis in exchange for favourable rulings for senior members. Judicial capture rarely produces a case in Mexico, and this one arrived as a US sanctions listing rather than a domestic prosecution.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2019

n: Roberto Sandoval Castaneda — Governor of Nayarit 2011–2017
d: Designated under the Global Magnitsky order for taking bribes from the CJNG and earlier from the Beltran Leyva organisation in exchange for information and protection, and for misappropriating state assets. His own attorney general, Edgar Veytia, had already pleaded guilty in Brooklyn two months earlier — the state's two senior law-enforcement figures reached the same finding by different routes.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 13818, May 2019

n: Erik Suniga Rodriguez — municipal mayor, the Los Pochos organisation
d: A serving mayor was designated as a significant foreign narcotics trafficker along with the organisation named after him, four associates and five Guatemalan companies. Treasury redesignated the group in 2024, noting a change of leadership and its members' continuing involvement in local politics.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, December 2019; redesignation under E.O. 14059, February 2024

n: Michel Martelly — President 2011–2016
d: Designated by the US Treasury for trafficking activity, including sponsoring and financing gangs, in a country where the gang system and the cocaine transit route have merged. Canada had sanctioned him earlier over gang financing. He denies the allegations; no court has heard them.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, August 2024; Global Affairs Canada sanctions, November 2022

n: Gustavo Petro — sitting President
d: The United States designated the sitting Colombian president under its illicit-drug order in October 2025, citing a rise in coca cultivation under his administration and the handling of intelligence channels. Colombia rejected the finding, and the two governments' assessments of the same period diverge sharply. This is an executive designation rather than a charge, and belongs on the map as one.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, October 2025; Government of Colombia response

n: The Assad family and the Fourth Division — the captagon designations
d: Three cousins of the president were designated by the US, UK and EU across March and April 2023 over captagon production and smuggling, alongside the manager of the Fourth Division's revenues and militia leaders in the south. Treasury put one Latakia facility's output at 84 million pills in 2020. The EU stated the trade had become a regime-led business model; the findings are executive and no court has heard them.
cite: OFAC designations under E.O. 13572 and 13582, March 2023; UK FCDO designations, March 2023; Council of the EU designations, April 2023

n: Amer Khiti — member of parliament and captagon logistics
d: A sitting member of the Syrian parliament was designated by the UK and the EU over companies used to produce, package and move captagon. Legislative office in this case is not protection bought from the trade but a position held inside it.
cite: UK FCDO designation, March 2023; Council of the EU designation, April 2023

n: Taliban shadow ministry — the 2012 Kingpin designation
d: A Taliban figure designated under the Kingpin Act in 2012 for his role in narcotics trafficking was, by late 2017, serving as the movement's shadow foreign minister and managing its relations with Iran. He also sits on the UN Security Council's 1988 sanctions list, which is the rare instance of the same person appearing on a drug list and a counter-terrorism list for the same conduct.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, November 2012; UN Security Council Resolution 1988 sanctions list

n: Los Cuellos Blancos del Puerto — the Callao judiciary
rank: supreme court judge, court president and judicial council
d: Wiretaps placed on a Callao trafficking organisation caught a different network on the same lines: a supreme court judge, the president of the Callao superior court and members of the judicial appointments council trading sentence reductions, promotions and favours. The judge fled to Spain, the court president was jailed, and the first conviction after a full trial came only in November 2025, seven years on. Several implicated judges were still sitting while under investigation.
cite: IDL-Reporteros audio releases from July 2018; Corte Superior Nacional de Justicia Penal Especializada, first trial verdict November 2025

n: Operacao Tacitus — Sao Paulo civil police and the PCC
d: Prosecutors allege a police chief, an officer and three investigators of the Sao Paulo civil police negotiated around 30 million reais in payments to shield PCC members from investigations, one of them producing a false document for the faction. Authorising the arrests, the judge wrote that no faction reaches the PCC's scale without the participation of public officials in the security services. The defence says the facts were investigated and shelved previously and calls the arrests arbitrary.
cite: Ministerio Publico de Sao Paulo, Operacao Tacitus, arrests December 2024

n: General Dom Hak — military intelligence chief
d: A two-star general was arrested with seven others after police found 35 kilograms of heroin and manufacturing equipment in a Phnom Penh house. The government burned the seizure publicly before prosecutors had begun, then released him within weeks for lack of evidence. It remains the highest-ranking Cambodian drug case to reach a court.
cite: Phnom Penh Municipal Court, charge and release October 2003

n: Mario Ruiz Massieu — Deputy Attorney General 1993–1994
d: The official who ran Mexico's counter-narcotics prosecutions moved about $9 million into Houston bank accounts in cash, carried by an aide on some twenty-five commercial flights. A Houston civil jury found the money was paid by traffickers, principally the Gulf Cartel, for protection. He fought extradition under house arrest for four years and killed himself in New Jersey in 1999 before the criminal case was tried.
cite: US civil forfeiture proceedings, S.D. Tex., jury finding 1997; extradition litigation 1995–1999

n: Proceso 8000 — the Samper campaign accounts
rank: head of state and campaign officials
d: Prosecutors established that the Cali cartel had put money into the 1994 presidential campaign; the campaign treasurer, the defence minister and the comptroller were convicted, and a congressional commission cleared the president himself in a vote his opponents called a whitewash. The United States revoked his visa. It is the earliest case on this map where a national election, rather than an agency, was the thing bought.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion, Proceso 8000, from 1995; Camara de Representantes vote, June 1996

n: General Antonio Indjai — armed forces chief of staff
d: The general who led the 2012 coup was charged in New York with conspiring to distribute cocaine and to arm the FARC, including a proposal to move their cocaine through the country and supply surface-to-air missiles in return. He was never surrendered. With the navy and air force chiefs charged in the same period, the entire senior command stood accused at once.
cite: US v. Indjai, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013

n: The vanished 975 kilograms
d: The director of the judicial police said 975 of 980 kilograms seized in November 2021 had disappeared from official custody, and that police and security personnel were suspected of taking it. One officer was arrested. The country had not tried a drug case since 2005, which is the context for a seizure evaporating rather than becoming evidence.
cite: Guinea-Bissau Policia Judiciaria statement, February 2022; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing record, 2009

n: The 2008 Lungi cocaine flight
d: A twin-engine aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine landed at Lungi airport in July 2008 marked with Red Cross insignia. The prosecutions that followed reached airport and security personnel alongside the foreign crew, and were described in US congressional testimony as historic for the region — the point of comparison being Guinea-Bissau, which had tried no drug case since 2005.
cite: Sierra Leone High Court convictions, 2009; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing, June 2009

n: Operation Black Tie — officials in the Nizic network
d: Twenty-three people were arrested in Sarajevo in April 2024 over trafficking and laundering for the inner circle of a kingpin already sentenced in the Netherlands. Europol stated that those detained included not only accomplices but corrupt officials identified as facilitators of the network. The case is Bosnia's first documented reach into the state layer of a Balkan cocaine organisation.
cite: Europol and Bosnian security agencies, Operation Black Tie, April 2024

n: Upakit Pachariyangkun — senator
d: A sitting senator was indicted on narcotics trafficking and laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok in 2022 and sanctioned by the US over support for the junta. His Thai-American son-in-law was among those arrested; the narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his residences. The case reaches from Shan State production into the Thai upper house.
cite: Thai Office of the Attorney General indictment, 2023; Narcotics Control Board seizures; OFAC designations of the associated network

n: Giulio Andreotti — seven-time Prime Minister
d: Prosecutors charged that he had put the influence of his office at Cosa Nostra's disposal in exchange for electoral support, and that the organisation expected him to fix the Maxi Trial, the case that had convicted 475 of its members for a heroin economy running through New York. He was acquitted in 1999 and again in 2003; the appellate judges found ties to mobsters before 1980 but held the limitation period had expired. The Court of Cassation closed the matter in 2004.
cite: Tribunale di Palermo, acquittal October 1999; Corte d'Appello 2003; Corte di Cassazione 2004

n: Federal judges of Oran and Salta
d: A federal judge in Oran was sentenced to 13 years in 2019 as head of an association that took money and property in exchange for rulings favouring traffickers. The same trafficker had bought a different federal judge in 2007, who was removed and convicted; that magistrate killed himself in 2020 as his arrest approached. A federal judge in Mendoza was separately charged over links to trafficking groups.
cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Salta, conviction of ex-judge Reynoso, March 2019; earlier conviction of judge Sola Torino, 2007

n: Caso Purga — the Guayas courts
d: A parallel file on judicial corruption in Guayas province charged judges alongside a former legislator described by prosecutors as the power behind the provincial courts. Testimony described payments arranged to obtain releases, including a failed attempt to free a former vice-president. Sentence reductions granted by prison-guarantee judges, outside their competence, were the recurring mechanism.
cite: Ecuadorian Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Purga, from 2024

n: Judge Amaury de Lima e Souza — criminal enforcement court, Juiz de Fora
d: Federal police arrested the judge of the criminal enforcement court in 2014 during an operation against an international trafficking route running from Bolivia through Paraguay into Minas Gerais and on to Rio and the north-east. Investigators found a series of rulings he had signed for traffickers, one granting house arrest to a defendant the prosecutors had charged. He was sentenced in 2022 to 24 years and four months.
cite: Tribunal de Justica de Minas Gerais, 5th criminal chamber, sentence October 2022; Policia Federal operation, June 2014

n: Cartel de la Toga — the Supreme Court bribery network
rank: supreme court presidents and anti-corruption prosecutor
d: Two former presidents of the Supreme Court, a sitting magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking payments to shelve or steer criminal proceedings against members of Congress, including men under investigation in the parapolitica files over ties to the AUC. One ex-president drew 16 years; another was sentenced to 10 in February 2026 with an Interpol red notice; the prosecutor was convicted in Colombia and separately in Miami. The bribes bought the appeal layer above the cases this map already records.
cite: Corte Suprema de Justicia de Colombia, Sala Especial, convictions 2021–2026; US v. Moreno Rivera, S.D. Fla., 2019

n: Prosecutor charged over Gulf Clan assets
d: A serving prosecutor was charged with lending her name to conceal property belonging to a front man for the Gulf Clan, the country's largest cocaine trafficking organisation, and placed under house arrest. The mechanism is the quiet one: not a case fixed, but title held.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion charge and house arrest order, July 2023

n: The Michoacanazo — mayors and officials released
d: Federal police arrested more than 30 state and municipal officials, including ten mayors, in May 2009 for alleged ties to La Familia Michoacana. Within two years every one of them had been released, the federal judiciary finding the prosecution's evidence insufficient. The episode set the federal government against the state and against its own courts, and is the clearest instance on this map of a mass capture case collapsing without a single conviction.
cite: Procuraduria General de la Republica prosecutions, May 2009; federal judicial releases 2009-2011; Mexican Law Review study of the case

n: Operation Eureka — 76 convictions
d: A Reggio Calabria bunker court convicted 76 defendants and acquitted seven in October 2025, in a case built from a 2023 carabinieri operation that seized three tonnes of cocaine and arrested 108 people. Prosecutors described three trafficking associations run by the most powerful Ionian 'Ndrangheta families. It is the counterweight to the capture entries: the same state whose Calabrian councils are dissolved for infiltration also runs the courts that convict at this scale.
cite: Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, Operation Eureka first-instance verdicts, October 2025; DDA Reggio Calabria and ROS carabinieri investigation, May 2023

n: Border Guard officers of the Vakhsh checkpoint
rank: border guard officers and provincial police
d: A military court in Khatlon sentenced five Border Guard Service officers to between three and 21 years, the longest for the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan frontier, in whose office investigators had found 20 kilograms of hashish. A senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day with 12 kilograms of heroin. Roughly 90 tonnes of heroin cross Central Asia each year and most seizures are of small dealers; this is the rank at which the record stops.
cite: Khatlon military court, sentences November 2012; State Committee for National Security statement, November 2012

n: The ambassador and the deputy interior minister
d: Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty in 2000 with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car. The following year the deputy interior minister was murdered, and prosecutors argued at trial that he was killed for refusing to pay for a 50-kilogram consignment. Estimates in 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of the country's economy.
cite: Kazakh authorities, arrest in Almaty 2000; Tajik prosecution case in the 2001 killing; UNODC and academic estimates

n: Harun Mwau — legislator and assistant transport minister
d: Designated by the US as a drug kingpin in 2011 while a sitting member of parliament. He had headed the national anti-corruption agency, funded a presidential campaign, and been appointed assistant transport minister with responsibility for container arrangements and the Ports Authority. He resigned after being named in parliament, has consistently denied the allegations, and was absolved by a police investigation researchers described as conducted in controversial circumstances.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, June 2011; Kenyan parliamentary naming and subsequent police inquiry

n: Jackie Selebi — national police commissioner and Interpol president
d: The head of the South African police, and simultaneously president of Interpol, was convicted of corruption in 2010 over payments from a drug trafficker and sentenced to 15 years. The wife of the state security minister was convicted separately in 2011 of conspiring to traffic. No other country on this map has convicted a serving Interpol president.
cite: South Gauteng High Court, conviction July 2010, sentence August 2010; Supreme Court of Appeal 2011; separate conviction of Sheryl Cwele, 2011

n: The protected heroin corridor
d: Researchers documented a trafficking system running for three decades with, in their words, a tight integration between ruling party figures and traffickers, and near-zero heroin seizures as the evidence of it. The principal named figure was designated abroad as a trafficker while remaining a prominent businessman at home. Family members were arrested in Portugal and Eswatini and one was shot dead in Maputo in 2012; none was ever charged in Mozambique.
cite: Global Initiative and ENACT research by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, 2018; LSE International Development working paper 18-190

n: Police command and airport security — the 2026 charges
d: After the country's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general stated that senior government officials were involved in trafficking. The national police charged the head of its Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport as an active participant. Twelve suspects were charged in the seizure case; a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking counts.
cite: Liberia National Police charges and Inspector General statements, 2026; indictment of the former vice-president, 2026

n: The minister of transport and aviation
d: The minister responsible for transport and aviation was dismissed after proceedings in the Lungi cocaine case indicated he had provided landing clearance for the aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms. The dismissal was administrative; the allegation itself was never tried.
cite: Sierra Leone government dismissal, 2008–2009; Africa Center for Strategic Studies review of the case

n: Operation Relentless — bribing the government that reported it
d: South American and West African traffickers were recorded paying senior Liberian officials to guarantee safe passage and storage for multi-tonne cocaine shipments. The officials reported the approaches and worked with the DEA instead, producing extraditions to New York and convictions there. The DEA called the cooperation from the highest levels of the Liberian government unprecedented, which is the measure of how rare that response is on this map.
cite: US v. Umeh, Salazar Castano, Kamara and others, S.D.N.Y., indictments and convictions from 2010
who: Latin American and West African traffickers

n: Gamboa Sanchez — Minister of Public Security and judge
rank: vice-minister of public security, later judge
d: A former Vice Minister of Public Security who later sat as a judge, designated by Treasury in August 2025 for facilitating the movement of tens of millions of dollars' worth of cocaine from Colombia through Costa Rica to the United States and Europe. Treasury's finding is what distinguishes him from the other officials here: he used his network of contacts inside the government to obtain information about ongoing counter-narcotics investigations. He was arrested in June 2025 on a US extradition request, weeks after Costa Rica's president signed a constitutional reform permitting the extradition of Costa Rican nationals for drug trafficking and terrorism — a change that made his own removal possible.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0227 and OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, 15 August 2025; Costa Rican arrest, 23 June 2025; constitutional reform on extradition signed May 2025

n: Caso Colorado — police officers on the Caribbean corridor
d: Investigators established regular telephone contact between an organisation holding the Caribbean lowland corridor and officers stationed at Guapiles and Cariari de Pococi. Some were recruited specifically to warn of raids, checkpoints and investigator movements in time for drugs to be moved or hidden. Five officers were charged before the specialised organised crime court.
cite: Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, case file 21-000115-0622-PE; Fiscalia Adjunta contra el Narcotrafico charges, 2026

n: The DNCD and the armed forces
d: Three senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency were arrested providing security to traffickers awaiting a shipment bound for Puerto Rico. A navy officer responsible for port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain; nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused in 2008 of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD personnel have been removed, around 200 of them suspected of trafficking, and the national police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010.
cite: DNCD arrests and dismissal statistics reported 2012-2013; Dominican prosecutions of navy and police personnel

n: The Escobar of the Sahara trial — legislators and a regional council president
d: A Casablanca court sentenced 29 people in June 2026 after a two-year trial, among them a construction figure and former head of a regional council who drew 12 years, and two former members of parliament from the governing party who drew 10 each. The case began with testimony from a jailed Malian trafficker who said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his 2019 arrest, and covered tonnes of cannabis resin moved across North Africa alongside Latin American cocaine. Charges included drug and gold trafficking, corruption and laundering; one defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.
cite: Casablanca Court of Appeal, verdicts 26 June 2026

n: Serving and former police officers — the 2025 designations
d: Two Guyanese law enforcement officers were designated on 5 June 2025: one serving, for arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers moving cocaine through the country, and one former officer wanted over the abduction of a policeman in 2024. Neither has been tried. Treasury noted that Guyana is a close US partner and that the State Department nonetheless treats corruption there as a significant obstacle to its own counter-narcotics effort — an ally and a problem named in the same paragraph. The network they served is recorded separately on the company layer.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation

n: The Phantom Squad
d: Guyana's most powerful trafficker ran an armed group that operated alongside the state during a period of killings in the mid-2000s, using construction and forestry businesses to launder cocaine proceeds moved from Colombia to the United States. He was convicted in New York and served 15 years. The squad's relationship to the government was examined publicly and never resolved in a Guyanese court.
cite: US v. Khan, E.D.N.Y., conviction and 15-year sentence; Guyanese public inquiries into the killings of 2002-2006

n: The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone
d: The government granted a Chinese company a concession in the Lao section of the Golden Triangle in 2007. Treasury later designated its head and his wife over heroin and methamphetamine trafficking and laundering. The US State Department reported that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations, that jurisdictional confusion between officials and zone security hinders investigation, and that no complicit official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.
cite: OFAC Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, January 2018; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report 2024

n: 'Criminals in uniform' — the constabulary and the black flights
d: After a Cessna loaded with 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby, the police commissioner said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and committed to removing them. The Australian-based organisers were convicted in Victoria and the pilot drew 18 years in a PNG jail; the officers alleged to have enabled the night flights were not charged. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has raised the same concern about infiltration of law enforcement there.
cite: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary statements, 2020; Victoria County Court sentences, July 2026; Lowy Institute analysis of Pacific trafficking

n: Ruben Rocha Moya — sitting Governor of Sinaloa
d: A sitting governor and nine other current and former Sinaloa officials, among them a senator, a state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary, police commanders and the mayor of Culiacan, were indicted in Manhattan in April 2026 over a protection arrangement with the Chapitos faction. Prosecutors allege he met the faction before the 2021 election and undertook to install friendly officials, that cartel members stole ballot boxes and intimidated rivals to secure his victory, and that he then let them consolidate control of state and local law enforcement. He rejects the accusations. Mexico said the extradition request lacked sufficient evidence and opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody. He announced his resignation on 1 May 2026, days after the indictment, calling it a political attack; the mayor of Culiacan stepped down in the same week.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026; Fiscalia General de la Republica statement, 2026; resignations reported 1-2 May 2026

n: The Culiacan municipal and police officials
rank: mayor, police commanders and a senator
d: Nine officials charged alongside the governor cover almost every layer of a single state: the mayor of the capital, a sitting senator, the state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary and several police commanders. One is additionally charged over the kidnapping of a DEA source and a relative, both of whom died. The indictment describes a complete political and police protection network rather than individual corruption.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026

n: Rubilio Orlando Palacios — anti-drug police official
d: The third official arrested with Guatemala's anti-drug chief and his deputy when all three travelled to the United States in 2005, charged in a three-count Washington indictment after a four-month DEA and Guatemalan investigation. The DEA administrator described them as Trojan horses for the addiction they were entrusted to prevent.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment November 2005; pleas 2006

n: The Fourth Criminal Court — Assad and the Fourth Division
rank: head of state, division commander and security chiefs
d: On 11 August 2026 the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced the deposed president to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and his brother, who commanded the Fourth Armoured Division, to death in absentia; six other officials received the same sentence in absentia. Only one defendant was present, a cousin who ran political security in Deraa and had been sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2011; he stood in a cage in prison uniform to hear it and has the right to appeal. Both brothers are in Russia with political asylum and Moscow has refused extradition. Opposition activists accuse the Fourth Division of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, and Western and regional governments treat it as the backbone of state captagon manufacture — but the convictions are for war crimes, not the trade. Human Rights Watch opposed the sentences and questioned whether a fair trial was guaranteed.
cite: Fourth Criminal Court, Damascus, judgment 11 August 2026, reported by SANA and international agencies; US Treasury designation of the Deraa political security head, April 2011; Human Rights Watch statement, August 2026

n: Nouh Zeaiter — the four-month sentence
rank: trafficker sanctioned by the US and EU
d: Sanctioned by the United States and the United Kingdom in 2023 over captagon manufacture and smuggling alongside relatives and associates of the Assad family, and already convicted in absentia by a Lebanese military court in 2021, which gave him life with hard labour, and sentenced to death in absentia in March 2024 for shooting at soldiers, one of whom was killed. The army took him in an ambush near Baalbek in November 2025 and called him one of the most dangerous wanted men in the country. In February 2026 the military court sentenced him to four months, finding him guilty in four minor matters — arms trafficking, shootings, unlicensed weapons and wearing military clothing — with weapons and radios confiscated. He denied trafficking and said he grew cannabis only between 2005 and 2008. The same court that had already sentenced him twice in absentia reached four months once he was in front of it.
cite: US and UK sanctions designations, 2023; Lebanese military court convictions in absentia, 2021 and March 2024; Lebanese Armed Forces arrest, 20 November 2025; military court sentence, February 2026

n: Louay al-Yasiri — a governor's son, pardoned
rank: son of a former governor, intelligence service employee
d: Sentenced to life in 2018 for drug offences, the son of a former provincial governor and himself an employee of the intelligence service. He was later pardoned and released. It is the clearest documented instance of a trafficker with direct government connections reaching an Iraqi court, and the sentence did not hold. Against it stands the volume the same judiciary produces: over 14,000 arrests in 2024, 144 death sentences for international traffickers and 434 life sentences for local offenders, and 973 convictions in the first quarter of 2025 alone.
cite: Iraqi court sentence, 2018, and subsequent pardon; Supreme Judicial Council and Ministry of Interior figures for 2024 and Q1 2025; UNODC seizure data

n: Revolutionary Court judges in the drug docket
d: Defence lawyers describe the courts that try drug cases as security-dominated and fast-tracking low-level defendants while leaving trafficking networks and higher-level operators untouched. One attorney who handled more than seventy drug cases documented the conduct of two named Tehran revolutionary court judges, one of whom he alleges was involved in financial corruption, and submitted a report with case files; lawyers who pursue such cases report being turned on themselves. With no independent forum, the allegation cannot be tested. Iran scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors, the joint highest on this map, and hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.
cite: Center for Human Rights in Iran, testimony of a defence attorney and analysis of drug sentencing, April 2025; Iranian judiciary announcements via Mizan Online

n: The tramadol trial — ten sentenced including security and intelligence officials
d: A court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people on 24 July 2020 over a transnational tramadol network, among them high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts reading the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums circulating among its members, some of it used in attempts to corrupt the judiciary and the security services. The conviction is real and the assessment that followed it is the point: with senior army and intelligence figures involved, enforcement runs into the institutions expected to carry it out.
cite: Court judgment, N'Djamena, 24 July 2020; Institute for Security Studies and ENACT analysis of the court documents, 2020; UNODC Sahel tramadol reporting, 2017

n: A mayor and 200 kilograms in his vehicle
d: A local mayor was arrested with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, an incident cited in investigative-journalism guidance for Africa as the model case of why a seizure is only the start: the work is unravelling the network behind the office rather than recording the arrest. No outcome is documented here. Niger sits on the Sahel corridor UNODC describes as a natural stopover between South America and Europe, and reporting on it carries physical risk to journalists.
cite: Global Investigative Journalism Network, Guide to Investigating Organized Crime in Africa, chapter on drug trafficking; UNODC Sahel trafficking assessments

n: Tramadol supplied to the presidential guard
rank: presidential guard and senior security officials
d: Reporting from Bangui, drawing on researchers, dealers and a former employee of the group, describes remnants of the Wagner organisation supplying tramadol to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia. Senior security officials are alleged to control the market, in which a consignment worth about $7,000 locally fetches up to $21,000 in Cameroon after roughly $4,000 is paid to Wagner and allied armed groups en route. A US-sponsored research centre assesses that the old Wagner has in effect taken over the state. Nothing has been charged. The country reports no update on an earlier case against a customs agent.
cite: Wall Street Journal reporting from Bangui, 12 July 2026; GI-TOC Central Africa Observatory report, June 2026; Africa Center for Strategic Studies assessment; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report, 2025

n: Nicolas Maduro — head of state
d: Charged in the Southern District of New York in March 2020 with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation and weapons counts, alongside a group of serving and former officials. The State Department reward for information leading to his arrest was raised twice, reaching $50 million in 2025. No trial has taken place and none of the evidence has been tested in court; the indictment is an accusation, and this map does not treat it as more than that.
cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; US Department of State Narcotics Rewards Program notices

n: Diosdado Cabello — legislature president, later Interior Minister
d: Designated by OFAC under the Kingpin Act in May 2018 and named in the 2020 SDNY indictment as a leader of the same structure. He has held the National Assembly presidency, the vice-presidency of the ruling party and, from 2024, the interior ministry. Both actions are executive and prosecutorial rather than judicial findings.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2018; US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., 2020

n: Maher al-Assad — commander, Fourth Armoured Division
d: The former president's brother, sanctioned by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union in 2023 over captagon production and export run through the division he commanded. The designations rest on intelligence findings and open-source investigation rather than a trial. After the government's collapse in December 2024 the production sites were opened to journalists and investigators, which corroborated the scale but not the individual attributions.
cite: US Treasury OFAC and UK Foreign Office designations, March 2023; EU Council Implementing Regulation 2023/720; Centre for Operational Analysis and Research captagon reporting

n: Porfirio Lobo Sosa — President 2010-2014
d: Named by US prosecutors as a recipient of trafficking proceeds during the cases against his son and successor, and placed on the State Department's Engel list of corrupt actors in 2021. He has never been charged. The allegations come from cooperating witnesses in other people's trials, which is the weakest category of evidence on this map and is marked as such.
cite: US Department of State section 353 corrupt and undemocratic actors list, July 2021; trial testimony in US v. Fabio Lobo and US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y.

n: Testimony naming a sitting president
d: Cooperating witnesses in the Guzman and Garcia Luna trials testified to bribes paid to a serving Mexican president. No charge has ever been brought, the testimony was not corroborated by documents, and the witnesses were negotiating their own sentences. It is recorded here because the claim was made under oath in a US federal court and because omitting it would misrepresent the trial record — not because it is established.
cite: Trial testimony, US v. Guzman Loera, E.D.N.Y., 2019, and US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., 2023

n: President Joao Bernardo Vieira and the 2009 killings
rank: head of state and armed forces chief
d: The president and the army chief of staff were killed within hours of each other in March 2009, during the period when UNODC described the country as at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state. No prosecution followed either killing. The link to the cocaine trade is the assessment of UNODC and of the UN Peacebuilding Support Office, not a court finding.
cite: UNODC Transnational Organized Crime in West Africa; UN Security Council reporting on Guinea-Bissau, 2009-2012

n: Nestor Reverol — head of the national anti-drug office, later Interior Minister
d: Indicted in the Eastern District of New York in 2015 for allegedly warning traffickers of raids and obstructing seizures while running the national anti-drug office. He was promoted to Interior Minister the following year and later to the electricity ministry. The indictment remains unexecuted.
cite: US v. Reverol Torres and Ordonez, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2015, unsealed August 2016

n: Abdelghani Hamel — Director-General of National Security
d: Removed after a 701-kilogram cocaine seizure at the port of Oran in May 2018 exposed the network behind it, and later convicted by a military court and by civilian courts on corruption and illicit enrichment counts. Several generals were convicted alongside him. The convictions are for corruption rather than narcotics, which is the record that exists; Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself.
cite: Algerian Blida military tribunal and Tipaza court judgments, 2019-2020; Algerian Ministry of Justice statements

n: Rana Sanaullah — provincial law minister
d: Arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force in July 2019 on a charge of transporting fifteen kilograms of heroin. The case collapsed and he was acquitted in 2022; the ANF officer who filed it later disowned the recovery. The episode is on this map as a documented instance of narcotics charges being deployed against a political opponent, which is a distinct failure mode from capture and belongs in the same record.
cite: Pakistan Anti-Narcotics Force case records; Lahore Special Court acquittal, 2022; Islamabad High Court proceedings

n: Abd al-Rahman Milad ('Bija') — coast guard commander
d: A serving coast guard unit commander at Zawiya, sanctioned by the UN Security Council in June 2018 over fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea. He was detained in Libya in 2020 and released without conviction in 2021. The same coastal networks move hashish and pharmaceuticals; the UN designation covers the smuggling economy rather than narcotics specifically.
cite: UN Security Council Committee on Libya sanctions listing, June 2018; UN Panel of Experts on Libya reports

n: Army and border officers in the captagon cases
d: Jordan's State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving captagon and weapons across the Syrian border, in cases running from 2022 onward. The army also conducted airstrikes inside Syria against production and storage sites. The convictions are the clearest evidence on this corridor that the protection extends into the interdicting force itself.
cite: Jordanian State Security Court judgments, 2022-2024; Jordanian Armed Forces statements

n: The 2017 official 'drug barons' list
d: The president read out a list of alleged drug traffickers in public in 2017 and ordered arrests; a regional commissioner and several public figures were named. Few prosecutions were completed and most of those detained were released. The episode is recorded as an assertion by a head of state, not as a set of findings.
cite: Tanzanian government statements, February 2017; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime East Africa reporting

n: Officials named in the compound designations
d: US and UK designations of Cambodian tycoons and companies over forced-labour fraud compounds have repeatedly described political protection as the reason the compounds operate openly. One designated figure was a serving senator. The designations are executive findings; Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of them.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025; UK sanctions designations

n: Customs and border officials in the 2021 designations
d: The largest single Magnitsky action ever taken against one country named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several of them in customs and border roles, over networks that included smuggling protection. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. The customs chokepoints on the Balkan route sit inside the same institutions.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Global Magnitsky designations, June 2021; European Commission Rule of Law reports on Bulgaria

n: State security links in the Belivuk prosecution
d: The prosecution of the Belivuk-Miljkovic group produced evidence that its members held state security identification and had access to protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. The case is running rather than concluded and the specific attributions remain contested in Serbian politics.
cite: Serbian Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime indictments, 2021-2024; Belgrade Higher Court proceedings

n: Rinascita-Scott — the 'Ndrangheta maxi-trial
d: Italy's largest organised crime trial since the Palermo maxi-trial: over 300 defendants, 207 convictions at first instance in November 2023. Those convicted included a former senator and lawyer who had acted for 'Ndrangheta figures, alongside police officers, officials and a former regional politician. Appeals are running.
cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia, Rinascita-Scott judgment, November 2023; Italian Direzione Nazionale Antimafia reporting

n: The judicial vetting
d: An EU-monitored vetting of every judge and prosecutor in the country, running since 2017, has removed or forced out roughly half of those assessed, mostly on unexplained-wealth grounds. It is the largest deliberate purge of a judiciary attempted in Europe and the clearest admission by a state that its own courts had been captured. Individual outcomes are administrative rather than criminal.
cite: Albanian Independent Qualification Commission and Special Appeal Chamber decisions; European Commission Albania progress reports

n: A Ultranza Py — prosecutors and judges
d: The 2022 investigation into a cocaine network moving product through the Hidrovia charged a serving prosecutor, court officials and figures connected to the legislature alongside the traffickers. One of the case's own prosecutors was later removed. Several principals fled before arrest.
cite: Paraguayan Ministerio Publico, Operacion A Ultranza Py case file, 2022-2024; Paraguayan Jurado de Enjuiciamiento de Magistrados

n: The dismantling of the anti-impunity capacity
d: The UN-backed anti-impunity commission that produced most of the country's trafficking-linked prosecutions was expelled in 2019, and by 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked those cases had left the country under threat of arrest. The cases they built, several of them on this map, no longer have a domestic forum. This is capture achieved by removing the prosecutor rather than buying the judge.
cite: UN International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) closure reporting, 2019; Inter-American Commission on Human Rights precautionary measures; US Department of State section 353 listings

n: Jose Luis Abarca — mayor of Iguala
d: Convicted of organised crime and kidnapping over the September 2014 disappearance of forty-three students, taken by municipal police acting for Guerreros Unidos. The Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts documented federal and state forces monitoring the events in real time. It remains the best-evidenced case on this map of a municipality operating as an arm of a trafficking organisation.
cite: Mexican federal court judgments, 2019 and 2022; GIEI Ayotzinapa reports; Mexican Comision para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia, 2022

n: Operacion Necora — Galicia
d: The operation that exposed the Galician rias as Europe's principal cocaine landing zone, run by tobacco-smuggling clans that had converted to cocaine for the Medellin and Cali organisations. Convictions followed for several clan leaders; a substantial number of defendants were acquitted, and the political and municipal protection alleged at the time was never proven in court. The landing infrastructure it described is still in use.
cite: Audiencia Nacional judgment, Operacion Necora, 1994; Spanish Fiscalia Antidroga historical reporting

n: The Punjab synthetic drug racket
rank: former deputy superintendent of police and political associates
d: A former deputy superintendent of police was convicted over a synthetic drug network valued by Indian investigators in the hundreds of crores, in a case that reached into Punjab's political class through an associate of a serving minister. The wider political allegations were never proven; the police conviction was.
cite: India Enforcement Directorate and Punjab Police case records; Special CBI Court, Mohali judgment

n: Charges brought against a critic of the drug war
d: A senator who had opened hearings into the killings was charged with drug offences in 2017 on the testimony of prison inmates and detained for almost seven years. Every charge was dismissed or ended in acquittal by 2023-2024 after witnesses recanted. This is the inverse of the pattern the rest of this layer records: not a state captured by the trade, but drug law used as an instrument against political opposition. Both are failures of the same institutions.
cite: Philippine Regional Trial Court, Muntinlupa, dismissals and acquittals, 2021-2024; UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention Opinion 2018

n: Militia and elected office in Rio de Janeiro
d: The 2024 arrests over the 2018 killing of a Rio city councillor reached a serving federal deputy, his brother a former state accounts councillor, and a former head of the civil police's intelligence bureau. Rio's militias began as off-duty police protection rackets and now hold territory alongside the drug commands, taxing the same residents. The case is at indictment stage.
cite: Brazilian Policia Federal and Procuradoria-Geral da Republica filings, March 2024; Supremo Tribunal Federal proceedings

n: Allegations against a former interior minister
d: A convicted organised crime figure published a long series of video statements from abroad in 2021 alleging that a former interior minister had protected trafficking networks, including a claim about a specific cocaine shipment. No charge followed in Turkiye and the allegations have never been tested. They are recorded because they were made publicly and in detail, and because the Susurluk file already on this map established the pattern they describe.
cite: Public statements by Sedat Peker, 2021; Turkish parliamentary opposition motions; no prosecution filed

n: A legislator arrested in a narcotics operation
d: A sitting deputy of the governing coalition was arrested in a police operation involving a cocaine sample, then released; parliamentary immunity was lifted and the case did not proceed to a verdict. Senegal's ports and airport sit on the West African route and the case is the only one to have reached the legislature.
cite: Senegalese Division des Investigations Criminelles case records, 2019; Senegalese National Assembly immunity proceedings

n: The 30th Precinct — New York
d: Thirty-three officers of one Harlem precinct were arrested for robbing dealers, reselling seized cocaine and perjury. Around 125 convictions were vacated. The Mollen Commission, reporting the same year, found that the department's internal affairs function had been structured to avoid finding what it eventually found.
cite: Mollen Commission Report on Police Corruption, City of New York, July 1994; S.D.N.Y. prosecutions, 1994-1996

n: Rampart CRASH — Los Angeles
d: An anti-gang unit that planted evidence, shot unarmed people and dealt in seized narcotics. More than 100 convictions were overturned and the city entered a federal consent decree that ran for twelve years. Several officers were convicted; several convictions were later reversed on appeal, which is part of the record.
cite: Los Angeles Board of Inquiry into the Rampart Area Corruption Incident, 2000; US v. City of Los Angeles consent decree, 2001

n: The Miami River Cops
d: Officers of the Miami Police Department robbed cocaine loads from the river and resold them; three men drowned fleeing one raid. Nineteen officers were convicted after three federal trials. The department had expanded rapidly in the preceding years with reduced screening, which the subsequent review identified as the enabling condition.
cite: US v. Garcia et al., S.D. Fla., 1986-1988; City of Miami internal review, 1988

n: Customs and Border Protection corruption
d: The largest federal law enforcement agency in the country records a continuous stream of officer prosecutions for waving loads through ports of entry, running to more than 200 corruption convictions across a decade. The agency's own integrity advisory panel found the internal affairs staffing inadequate to the caseload and said so in public.
cite: CBP Integrity Advisory Panel final report, 2016; CBP Office of Professional Responsibility annual statistics; DOJ prosecution records
who: Mexican cartels at ports of entry

n: The Philadelphia narcotics field unit
d: Six officers were tried federally for robbing dealers and falsifying reports and were acquitted in 2015. The city nonetheless vacated around 1,000 convictions the unit had produced and paid several million dollars in civil settlements. An acquittal and a mass vacatur in the same case is the clearest illustration on this map of how differently the criminal and civil standards resolve.
cite: US v. Liciardello et al., E.D. Pa., verdict May 2015; Philadelphia District Attorney's Office conviction review; city civil settlements

n: The Camden narcotics squad
d: Officers planted drugs and fabricated reports; around 200 cases were dismissed and the city later dissolved its police department entirely and rebuilt it under county control. It is one of very few instances anywhere on this map of an institution being abolished rather than reformed.
cite: US v. Bayard et al., D.N.J., 2010; New Jersey Attorney General review; City of Camden police dissolution, 2013

n: Operation Tiberius — the Metropolitan Police
d: An internal Metropolitan Police report, written in 2002 and leaked in 2014, concluded that organised crime networks had been able to infiltrate the force at will, naming officers connected to specific families. It was never published, no prosecutions followed from it, and its findings have not been tested in any forum. It is the most senior internal assessment of its kind in a Western police service.
cite: Metropolitan Police Operation Tiberius report, 2002 (leaked 2014); UK Home Affairs Select Committee questioning, 2014

n: Eirik Jensen — head of the Oslo police narcotics unit
d: The officer who ran Oslo's narcotics section for years was convicted of aggravated corruption and of complicity in importing around fourteen tonnes of hashish with an informant he had run, and sentenced to twenty-one years. The Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.
cite: Oslo District Court 2017 and Borgarting Court of Appeal 2020 judgments; Norwegian Supreme Court refusal, 2021

n: Police and security service leaks to the networks
rank: police employees and a security service officer
d: Swedish courts have convicted police employees of passing information from law enforcement registers to criminal networks, and separately convicted a Security Service officer of unauthorised disclosure. Police reporting names insider access to registers as a systematic vulnerability rather than an isolated failure.
cite: Swedish district court judgments, 2021-2024; Polismyndigheten and Sakerhetspolisen public reporting

n: Customs and port officers at the northern terminals
d: Prosecutions at Hamburg and Bremerhaven have convicted customs officers and terminal employees of clearing containers and passing scanner information. German federal police assessments treat port-side insider access as the decisive vulnerability in the northern European cocaine flow, as Belgian and Dutch assessments do for Antwerp and Rotterdam.
cite: Hamburg and Bremen Landgericht judgments, 2020-2024; Bundeskriminalamt Rauschgiftkriminalitat Bundeslagebild

n: The BAC Nord case — Marseille
d: Officers of the northern Marseille anti-crime brigade were charged with stealing seized cannabis, money and phones from the estates they policed. Convictions followed after a long procedural fight; several charges fell away. The estates in question are the same ones on this map's group layer.
cite: Tribunal correctionnel de Marseille judgments, 2015-2021; Inspection generale de la police nationale reporting

n: The Vught escape plot
d: Prosecutors alleged a plan to free the principal defendant in the Marengo trial from the country's highest-security prison, involving contacts around the legal and custodial system. It followed the murders of the trial's crown witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist. The Dutch state's response was to harden the prison regime, which is a measure of how far the threat was assessed to reach.
cite: Dutch Openbaar Ministerie statements and Rechtbank Amsterdam proceedings, 2022-2024

n: The Noor 1 case
d: Two tonnes of heroin arrived at Piraeus aboard a tanker and part of the load disappeared before it was secured. Convictions followed for the vessel's operators and associates; the Greek parliament held hearings on how the load moved through the port. It remains the largest single seizure in Greek history and the case that established Piraeus as an entry point rather than a transit stop.
cite: Greek Court of Appeal judgments, 2016-2019; Hellenic Parliament committee proceedings

n: Police leaks to criminal organisations
d: Israeli courts have convicted serving officers of passing investigative material to crime organisations, in cases brought by the justice ministry's police investigations department. The organisations receiving the material are the same families mapped in the group layer.
cite: Israeli Department for Investigation of Police Officers (Mahash) case records; district court judgments, 2019-2024

n: Carabineros narcotics units
d: Chilean prosecutors have charged officers of the Carabineros with reselling seized narcotics and protecting distribution in Santiago and the northern border region, in a series of cases running alongside the institution's wider post-2019 crisis. Chile's role shifted in this period from consumer market to transit route.
cite: Chilean Fiscalia Nacional and Fiscalia de Alta Complejidad case records, 2020-2024

n: Narcotics police and enforcement officers
d: Malaysia's anti-corruption commission has prosecuted narcotics officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized product, in cases concentrated in Johor and the Klang valley. The country sits on the Golden Triangle export route and hosts the region's busiest transhipment port.
cite: Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission prosecution records, 2018-2024; Malaysian sessions court judgments

n: Police and political links in the Madush case
d: The arrest in Dubai of a Sri Lankan trafficking figure produced photographs of him with police officers, entertainers and politicians at a party, triggering suspensions and an inquiry. He was killed in police custody in 2020 before any of it was tested. The inquiry did not conclude.
cite: Sri Lanka Police Special Investigation Unit reporting, 2019-2020; Sri Lankan Human Rights Commission inquiry into the custodial death

n: The Teknaf yaba campaign and its aftermath
d: The anti-drug campaign on the Myanmar border produced hundreds of killings in police custody or 'crossfire'. A former officer-in-charge of the Teknaf station and several colleagues were sentenced to death in 2022 for the killing of a retired army major who had filmed them. The convictions are for murder; the drug economy the campaign targeted was not disrupted.
cite: Cox's Bazar District and Sessions Judge Court verdict, January 2022; UN OHCHR statements on Bangladesh drug operations

n: The drug war killings
d: Between 6,000 and more than 30,000 people were killed in anti-drug operations from 2016, depending on whether the count is the government's or that of human rights monitors. The International Criminal Court authorised an investigation into them as crimes against humanity in 2021, and the former president was surrendered to the Court in 2025. The trade itself continued through the campaign.
cite: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authorisation, September 2021, and arrest warrant proceedings, 2025; UN OHCHR report on the Philippines, 2020

n: Border and law enforcement officers
